items.content: The European AI Office supports the development and adoption of trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (AI) solutions, while protecting people against risks. The European AI Office was established within the European Commission as the foundation for a single AI governance system. It supports the EU approach to AI , playing a key role in implementing the AI Act – especially for general-purpose AI (GPAI) – guaranteeing the health, safety and fundamental rights of people and providing legal certainty to businesses. It also enforces the rules for GPAI models and supports the governance bodies in Member States in their tasks. This is underpinned by the powers given to the Commission by the AI Act, including the ability to conduct evaluations of GPAI models, request information and measures from model providers, and apply sanctions. The AI Office also promotes an innovative ecosystem of trustworthy AI , to reap the societal and economic benefits. It ensures a strategic, coherent and effective European approach to AI at international level , becoming a global reference point. The Structure of the AI Office The AI Office employs more than 125 staff, including technology specialists, administrative assistants, lawyers, policy specialists, and economists. It has 6 units and 2 advisers, reflecting its mandate: “Excellence in AI and Robotics” - unit A1 “Regulation and Compliance” - unit A2 “AI Safety” - unit A3 “AI Innovation and Policy Coordination” - unit A4 “AI for Societal Good” - unit A5 "AI in Health and Life Science" - unit A6 Lead Scientific Adviser International Affairs Adviser Tasks of the AI Office Supporting the AI Act and enforcing general-purpose AI rules The AI Office makes use of its expertise to support the implementation and enforcement of the AI Act by: Contributing to the coherent application of the AI Act across the Member States, including the set-up of advisory bodies at EU level, facilitating support and information exchange Developing tools, methodologies and benchmarks for evaluating capabilities and reach of general-purpose AI models, and classifying models with systemic risks Drawing up state-of-the-art codes of practice to detail out rules, in cooperation with leading AI developers, the scientific community and other experts Preparing guidance and guidelines, implementing and delegated acts , and other tools to support effective implementation of the AI Act and monitor compliance with the regulation Investigating possible infringements of the rules, including inspections, requests for technical documentation and access to models in order to assess models' capabilities Requesting providers to take corrective action and, in case of infringement, restrict the public availability of a model and issue direct fines for non-compliance Strengthening the development and use of trustworthy AI The AI Office, in collaboration with relevant public and private actors and the startup community, contributes to fostering trustworthy AI across the EU by: Advancing actions and policies to reap the societal and economic benefits of AI across the EU Providing advice on best practices and enabling ready-access to AI sandboxes, real-world testing and other European support structures for AI uptake Encouraging innovative ecosystems of trustworthy AI to enhance the EU’s competitiveness and economic growth Aiding the Commission in leveraging the use of transformative AI tools and reinforcing AI literacy Fostering international cooperation At international level, the AI Office contributes to a strategic, coherent, and effective EU approach, by: Promoting the EU’s approach to trustworthy AI , including collaboration with similar institutions worldwide Fostering international cooperation and governance on AI, contributing to a global approach to AI Supporting the development and implementation of international agreements on AI Cooperation with institutions, experts and stakeholders The AI Office collaborates with Member States and the wider expert community through dedicated platforms: The European Artificial Intelligence Board (AI Board) is a key advisory body supported by the AI Office that includes representatives from each EU Member States and the European Centre for Algorithmic Transparency (ECAT). The AI Board’s primary role is to ensure the effective implementation of the AI Act across the EU by coordinating national authorities, sharing technical and regulatory expertise and providing advice on AI policy, innovation, and international partnerships. The Scientific Panel of independent experts ensures a strong link with the scientific community. Further technical expertise is gathered in an Advisory Forum , representing a balanced selection of stakeholders, including industry, startups and Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs), academia, think tanks and civil society. The AI Office also oversees the AI Pact , which allows businesses to engage with the Commission and other stakeholders to share best practices and join activities. This engagement has started before the AI Act entered into force and allows businesses to plan ahead and prepare for the full implementation of the AI Act. To stay up to date and register, check the AI Pact events . The Apply AI Alliance is the main coordination forum bringing together AI providers, industry leaders, academia and the public sector to ensure policy actions are grounded in the real-world needs. Closely connected to the Alliance, an AI Observatory will track AI trends and assess impact of AI in specific sectors. Initiatives promoting the development and adoption of AI The AI Office actively supports innovators through policies and initiatives that spur growth across the EU: The AI Continent action plan , launched in April 2025, explains how to harness the untapped potential of EU researchers and industries, turning EU strengths – such as unparalleled talent and strong traditional industries – into AI accelerators. The plan promotes economic growth and competitiveness in areas such as healthcare, cars, science. The Apply AI Strategy , launched in October 2025, complements the action plan. It aims to boost AI adoption and innovation across Europe, particularly among SMEs. It is designed to enhance the competitiveness of strategic sectors and strengthen the EU’s tech sovereignty. In June 2026, the 'AI omnibus' (part of the Digital Simplification Package ) was adopted, introducing targeted amendments to the AI Act to ensure the rules remain clear, simple, and innovation-friendly. The amendments entered into force on 27 July. The ‘ GenAI4EU ' initiative, part of the 2024 AI innovation package , contributes to the development of novel use cases and emerging applications in 14 industrial sectors and the public sector. Other initiatives aimed at boosting the development and uptake of AI are: AI Factories Testing and Experimentation Facilities (TEFS) and sandboxes European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs) AI skills and literacy Job opportunities and collaboration The AI Office recruits talent from a wide range of backgrounds for policy, technical and legal roles and administrative support. To apply, complete the Expression of Interest Form . For inquiries, please contact us at the following addresses: Recruitment: CNECT-AIOFFICE-RECRUITMENT@ec.europa.eu General Inquiries: CNECT-AIOFFICE@ec.europa.eu Important: These email addresses are for inquiries only. Applications must be submitted through the dedicated form, not via email. Quick Links Any question on the AI Act? items.title: DigitalEU at Web Summit 2026: Supporting businesses and startups to grow and innovate
items.summary: This year, DG Connect will be at Web Summit in Lisbon from 10 to 12 November, with two Masterclasses focusing on EU support for businesses working with AI and on how Europe’s data spaces can help SMEs grow and innovate. Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen will also be present, taking part in a fireside chat on Europe’s technological sovereignty on Centre Stage on 10 November. During our Masterclasses, EU digital policy experts will explain the opportunities to access and use data from connected products and the support available at EU level through the EU Data Act. They will also present the practical support available to AI professionals and businesses, including regulatory guidance, testing facilities, infrastructure, expertise, funding and tools. A group of DigitalEU Ambassadors will also join us in Lisbon, creating content and sharing their perspectives from Web Summit. Other Commission services and EU bodies will also be present with Masterclasses, panels, meetups and stands.
items.content: This year, DG Connect will be at Web Summit in Lisbon from 10 to 12 November, with two Masterclasses focusing on EU support for businesses working with AI and on how Europe’s data spaces can help SMEs grow and innovate. Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen will also be present, taking part in a fireside chat on Europe’s technological sovereignty on Centre Stage on 10 November. During our Masterclasses, EU digital policy experts will explain the opportunities to access and use data from connected products and the support available at EU level through the EU Data Act. They will also present the practical support available to AI professionals and businesses, including regulatory guidance, testing facilities, infrastructure, expertise, funding and tools. A group of DigitalEU Ambassadors will also join us in Lisbon, creating content and sharing their perspectives from Web Summit. Other Commission services and EU bodies will also be present with Masterclasses, panels, meetups and stands. You can find DG GROW at stand E415 and HaDEA at stand E418, both in Pavilion 4, and EuroHPC at stand E405. Check out the agenda below to learn more about EU activities at this year’s Web Summit. AGENDA 10 November 11:05-11:25 – Fireside chat with EVP Virkkunen Has Europe’s tech moment arrived? Europe has an ambition to become a global tech powerhouse, whilst also setting the rules for the digital economy. Can Europe build a technology ecosystem that competes with the US and China while establishing the right governance approach through its rules? In this talk the EU Commission's EVP Henna Virkkunen discusses the EU’s drive for tech sovereignty, from AI and cloud to chips and digital infrastructure, alongside its efforts to regulate the platforms and AI systems reshaping society. 12:00-12:45 – DG CONNECT Masterclass Data spaces for SMEs: Turning shared data into value How can Europe’s data spaces help your SMEs grow and innovate? Explore new opportunities to access and use data from connected products and learn about the support available at EU level. 11 November 12:10 – 12:30 – EUIPO Panel The new financing frontier: How intellectual property unlocks capital. This discussion will examine how IP-backed finance can help innovative companies access capital and scale their businesses. 14:30-15:15 – DG CONNECT Masterclass Building AI in Europe: Practical Support for Innovators Europe is building an AI innovation ecosystem designed to help companies turn ideas into real-world solutions. Join this Masterclass to explore EU support, from regulatory guidance to access to infrastructure, funding and more. 15:30-16:15 – HaDEA Masterclass Investing in technological sovereignty: EU funding for your project Join HaDEA’s workshop to discover EU funding opportunities for your next project. Learn how EU funding is supporting technological sovereignty, meet representatives of the European Commission and get inspired by EU-funded projects. 16:00-16:45 – EuroHPC Masterclass Level up for free: Access EU supercomputing, AI & quantum resources Discover how industry can access Europe’s supercomputers, AI Factories and quantum computers for free. Learn about access opportunities, applications and support available through EuroHPC JU. Please be aware that attendance is first-come, first-served. 12 November 13:00 – 13:25 – EUIPO & INPI Meetup Startup & Creator IP Meetup This informal gathering will bring together startups, entrepreneurs and creators to exchange views on intellectual property and expand their networks. Last update 3 November 2026 Print as PDF

items.content: Featured projects On the evening of Sep 30, 2026, PyTorchKR and XCENA co-hosted KVCache Meetup Korea. PyTorchKR is a major AI/ML community in Korea, and XCENA is a startup that focuses on CXL (Compute Express Link). Tensormesh, the company behind LMCache, also sponsored the event. Speakers from XCENA, SK hynix, FuriosaAI, and LMCache shared their work on large language model (LLM) inference and KV Cache optimization. LLM inference runs a language model to generate output. KV Cache stores attention data for reuse during inference. Attendees at KVCache Meetup Korea 2026. Talks covered CXL memory expansion, GPU and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) bottlenecks, request scheduling on RNGD, and LMCache MP Mode. The sessions showed how hardware and serving software handle KV Cache in different ways. Serving software processes requests that run a model. Registration and Opening The program combined technical talks with opportunities for attendees to connect. Attendees who wanted to join the networking chose up to two interest stickers at registration. The five categories were Model, Serving, Infra, Hardware, and Memory. Attendees chose their interest stickers at registration. PyTorchKR organizer Junghwan Park and XCENA CPO Juhyun Kim opened the event. The speakers were Jooho Lee from XCENA, Sejin Oh from SK hynix, Donghun Lee from FuriosaAI, and Baoloong Mao from LMCache. They shared their experiences and approaches. Junghwan Park from PyTorchKR (left) and Juhyun Kim, CPO at XCENA (right), welcomed the attendees. CXL and KV Cache Storage: Jooho Lee, XCENA The session “CXL for KVCache” started with the basics of CXL and memory expansion. Jooho Lee explained how CXL expands the memory space that CPUs can access with load/store instructions. He also described a setup where multiple hosts use a memory pool and introduced Maru . Maru is a high-performance KV Cache storage engine that XCENA released as an open-source project. It helps LLM inference use shared CXL memory efficiently. Jooho Lee from XCENA presented “CXL for KVCache.” The KV Cache design combined DRAM and SSD storage in a CXL memory pool. It kept frequently used cache in DRAM and less frequently used cache on SSDs. Maru connects the inference engine to these storage layers. Optimizing LLM inference requires more than storing a large amount of cache. The path and cost of moving cache to the GPU also matter. The talk also covered splitting computation for experts in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models between a GPU and MX1. Experts are specialized parts of a model. The design places some weights in memory near MX1 and processes them there. It transfers intermediate values, called activations, and computation results instead of the full weights. The session started with KV Cache storage and also covered weight placement and ways to reduce data movement. GPU Compute and HBM Bandwidth: Sejin Oh, SK hynix Sejin Oh presented “Analyzing Utilization of GPU and HBM in LLM Serving Systems.” The talk examined how prefill and decode use system resources. Prefill processes the prompt, and decode generates output tokens. The session presented Roofline analysis alongside measurements from a running system. Roofline analysis compares compute and memory bandwidth limits. Sejin Oh from SK hynix presented the analysis of GPU compute and HBM bandwidth. The experiments used two H100 GPUs, Llama 3.1 8B, and vLLM. GPU compute use was high during the main projection operations in prefill. During decode, HBM bandwidth use was high. The experiments also explained the difference between TTFT and TPOT. TTFT measures the time to the first output token. TPOT measures the time per output token. Reusing KV Cache reduces computation during prefill. After that reduction, memory bandwidth can become the bottleneck. Whether a service needs more memory capacity or bandwidth depends on its input and output lengths, batch size, and other operating conditions. Scheduling and KV Cache on RNGD: Donghun Lee, FuriosaAI FuriosaAI is building Furiosa-LLM, its own inference engine for running LLMs on RNGD. In “LLM Inference Engine for RNGD,” Donghun Lee shared engineering problems from building the engine, including request scheduling and KV Cache management. He followed each request from arrival to execution. He explained PagedAttention for KV Cache blocks, Continuous batching for active requests, and Chunked prefill for smaller prompt segments. He also introduced buckets, or tensor shapes compiled before execution. Donghun Lee from FuriosaAI explained how to share KV Cache outside a node. Combining requests into one batch increases throughput, or the number of requests processed over time. Larger batches can need larger buckets and increase latency, or response delay. Furiosa-LLM measures the execution cost on the actual hardware. It merges two batches when the combined cost is lower than processing them separately. The decision also accounts for the context length of each request and the cost of padding. Padding fills unused positions in a fixed tensor shape. The talk compared the benefit of cache reuse with the cost of transferring it. The slides used a 12,370-token prompt, with one request at a time and three measurements for each condition. Retrieving the host cache and generating the first token took about 92 ms. Recomputing the cache took about 900 ms. Under those test conditions, retrieving the host cache was faster. He also explained how to overlap cache transfer with computation at each layer. The benefit depends on the amount of data transferred and the available bandwidth. Experimental features included a network-shared cache and running prefill and decode on separate resources. He also discussed plans for future expansion. ‘LMCache: A Unified KV Cache Management Layer with Multi-Platform Architecture’: Baoloong Mao, LMCache LMCache maintainer and core architect Baoloong Mao presented “A Unified KV Cache Management Layer with Multi-Platform Architecture.” LMCache is an open-source KV Cache project created by the team that founded Tensormesh . He explained how LMCache connects different inference engines with storage systems and hardware. He focused on MP Mode, which moves cache management from inside the inference engine into a separate process. Baoloong Mao from LMCache introduced the unified KV Cache layer and MP Mode. In MP Mode, CUDA IPC allows processes to share GPU memory. IPC means communication between processes. The processes exchange control information such as block IDs. They use a shared CPU memory pool within a node to reduce duplicate storage. MP Mode also reads and loads data from several storage layers in parallel. This design separates inference computation from cache I/O, or data transfers, to reduce competition for resources. The session also covered deployment and operations. Topics included deployment on Kubernetes and monitoring cache hit rates and cache lifetimes. A cache hit means that the requested data is available. The talk also covered isolating failures between inference and cache processes. External plugins allow connections to more storage systems and devices. Q&A and Networking In the Q&A session, the speakers returned to the stage to answer questions from attendees. Questions included separating prefill and decode, compared with mixed batching. Mixed batching processes prefill and decode work together. Attendees also asked about the roles of LMCache and the cache features built into vLLM. Another topic was the plan to extend MP Mode across multiple nodes. The speakers answered live questions together after the talks. After the Q&A, attendees from different fields gathered in small groups to talk. Their interest stickers helped them find people with similar interests. Speakers and attendees exchanged ideas and heard different perspectives. Conversations also continued around the CXL server from XCENA at the venue. Attendees examined the hardware up close and asked questions. They linked the memory expansion techniques from the talks to the hardware on display. Attendees talked during the networking session. Feedback from 72 Survey Responses The following summary draws on 72 survey responses. All numbers and percentages below use the survey responses as their base. Some questions allowed multiple selections. Event satisfaction and work experience by role, based on 72 survey responses. In the feedback questions, 48 respondents selected the program as a positive point (66.7%). The venue and facilities received 30 selections (41.7%). The atmosphere for conversations and the event timing each received 22 selections (30.6%). This question allowed multiple selections. Respondents gave positive feedback on the talks and the chance to meet other attendees. Repeated comments mentioned microphone quality and volume, screen visibility from the back rows, and limited space. Some respondents also asked for interpretation or translation to help them follow the English talks. Some respondents also asked for a dedicated session where developers in the same field can talk. Requests for future events included real production examples, vLLM and SGLang internals, compilers for neural processing units (NPUs), recent inference optimization techniques, and demos. Respondents wanted details about problems, trial and error, and solutions from real deployments. They asked speakers to explain these experiences, as well as their products. Group photo from KVCache Meetup Korea. PyTorchKR will use this feedback to plan and run future events. Thank you to everyone who joined the event on a weekday evening. The organizers also thank the speakers who shared their knowledge and experience. Thank you to PyTorchKR and XCENA for organizing the event, and to Tensormesh for its support.

items.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
items.summary: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports

AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. Microsoft Research StorY OptiMind: When the system meets the floor A three‑month pilot in a Midwestern bottling plant shows what happens when AI moves beyond chat and into decision-making, where constraints shift, stakes are real, and answers must hold. Learn more Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use 1. Use Flint in your chat Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation. Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns. 2. Build an interactive app with Flint Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas. Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa. 3. Create bespoke interactions To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks. Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes. How it works Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level: Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates. Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable c and cost effective. This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards. Try it now! Video playback requires cookie consent Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery. App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab) . Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app. Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab) , design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary. items.content: From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles Thanks: Equal supervision Equal contribution Paulius Skaisgiris Email: paulius.skaisgiris@tuwien.ac.at Affiliation: Institute of Logic and Computation, TU Wien, Austria 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Institute for Application-Oriented Knowledge Processing, JKU Linz, Austria Department of Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity, University of Klagenfurt, Austria Institute for Machine Learning, JKU Linz, Austria Institute for Symbolic Artificial Intelligence, JKU Linz, Austria 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Institute for Machine Learning, LIT AI Lab, Department of Virtual Morphology, Clinical Research Institute Medical AI, JKU Linz, Austria Thomas Pammer Email: tpammer@faw.jku.at Affiliation: Veronika Semmelrock Email: veronika.semmelrock@aau.at Affiliation: Mykyta Ielanskyi Email: ielanskyi@ml.jku.at Affiliation: Maximilian Heisinger Email: maximilian.heisinger@jku.at Affiliation: Erich Kobler Email: erich.kobler@jku.at Affiliation: Abstract Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation has substantially improved the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, including code generation, data analysis, and exam-style question answering. Despite these advances, purely neural LLMs continue to struggle with elementary logical reasoning problems and lack the determinism, soundness, and reliability characteristic of symbolic reasoning systems. Conversely, classical symbolic methods such as SAT solving and exact cover guarantee correctness and completeness, but require problems to be expressed in highly specialized formal encodings, limiting their applicability to natural language inputs. In this work, we present a synergistic neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by combining neural semantic parsing with deterministic exact cover reasoning. Given a Zebra-style logic puzzle in natural language, an LLM translates entities and constraints into structured tool calls that construct an exact cover instance. A symbolic solver then computes the solution and provides feedback to iteratively refine invalid, under- or overconstrained encodings, exploiting the uniqueness property of Zebra puzzles. We conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple parameter scales, post-training paradigms, and LLM families. The results demonstrate that our hybrid approach consistently outperforms strong plain neural baselines, including CoT prompting, as well as recent neuro-symbolic methods. 1 1 1 Code is available at https://codeberg.org/bilai-ss25-booleguru-llm/zebrallm . 1 Introduction Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs) lie at the core of many real-world decision-making tasks, including scheduling, planning, resource allocation, and configuration, making them a fundamental abstraction in AI research ( Russell and Norvig, 1995 ; Mackworth, 1977 ; Nadel, 1989 ; Knuth, 2016 ; Knuth, 2020 ; Knuth, 2025 ) . While symbolic methods such as SAT and constraint solvers can guarantee correctness and completeness, their practical deployment critically depends on constructing effective formal encodings – a process that remains difficult even for domain experts ( Heisinger et al., 2024 ) . Translating informal problem descriptions into a structured encoding requires substantial modeling expertise as small representational choices can dramatically impact solver performance and tractability. As a result, research often studies simplified yet representative proxy domains such as logic puzzles (e.g. Sudoku or Zebra Puzzles), which capture essential combinatorial and relational reasoning challenges while providing clean semantics, controllable complexity, and objectively verifiable solutions ( Dechter and Pearl, 1987 ; Prosser, 1993 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; White et al., 2025 ) . This reliance on structured benchmark domains aligns naturally with recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), which are increasingly applied to tasks requiring the construction of structured symbolic solutions from unstructured inputs. Such domains include mathematical reasoning ( Hendrycks et al., 2021b ) , programming ( Hendrycks et al., 2021a ) , planning ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and logic puzzle solving ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Chollet et al., 2025 ) . A shared characteristic of these problems is that, although discovering solutions is challenging, their correctness can be verified algorithmically. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards post-training has therefore emerged as a standard approach for optimizing models directly against symbolic verifiers ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . The resulting thinking LLMs produce Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning traces enabling inference-time scaling. Figure 1: Visualization of NeuralExactCover . A puzzle instance is combined with our prompt template and processed by an LLM that harmonizes attributes, extracts entities and clues, and translates clues into an exact cover encoding. The symbolic MiniExact solver then solves the encoding and provides iterative feedback on failures to refine the generated tool calls. This loop continues until a unique solution is found or the retry limit is reached, after which the solution is converted into plain text. Zebra Puzzles are among recent benchmarks to test the reasoning capabilities of LLMs ( Lin et al., 2025 ; White et al., 2025 ) . They consist of lists of entities, properties, and attributes as well as clues; the goal is to infer the relations of attributes and entities from the given information. Lin et al. (2025) find that scaling the model size does not help beyond a certain level of complexity which is defined by the puzzles’ solution space. This manifests in generalist LLMs faring extremely well on simple Zebra Puzzles while struggling with more complex ones. Longer reasoning traces appear to be more helpful with these problems than larger models. However, these longer traces present additional challenges such as high frequency noise ( Radler et al., 2025 ) and increased chance of hallucination ( Mei et al., 2025 ) . To address the reasoning limitations of purely neural models, recent neuro-symbolic approaches increasingly combine LLM-based semantic parsing with symbolic solvers to enforce logical consistency ( Dinu et al., 2024 ) . Prior work explores both agentic formulations that iteratively generate solver-compatible programs and solver-centric pipelines that translate natural language inputs into formal constraint specifications solved using SAT, SMT, CSP, or ASP techniques ( Szeider, 2025 ; Pan et al., 2023 ; Ye et al., 2023 ; Eiter et al., 2025 ) . Notably, Logic.py ( Kesseli et al., 2025 ) translates natural language into a domain-specific representation solved by an exact constraint solver, incorporating iterative error feedback to the LLM. This coupling of semantic parsing and symbolic solving consistently outperforms LLMs on Zebra Puzzle-style benchmarks. In this work, we present an integrated neuro-symbolic framework called NeuralExactCover that combines LLM-based semantic parsing with deterministic exact cover solving for reliable logical reasoning over plain text Zebra-style puzzles. Our main contributions are as follows: • We introduce and adapt an exact cover encoding for efficient symbolic solving of Zebra-style logic puzzles. • We introduce a neuro-symbolic framework that leverages LLMs as a translation layer for an exact cover solver and re-applies symbolic results as feedback to the LLM. • We introduce the ZebraExtreme dataset, extending ZebraLogic ( Lin et al., 2025 ) with even more challenging problems of size up to 8 × 10 8\times 10 entities and properties. 2 Background and Preliminaries 2.1 Exact Cover Given a collection S S of subsets of a set 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , the exact cover problem is about finding a subcollection 𝒮 ∗ ⊆ 𝒮 \mathcal{S}^{*}\subseteq{\mathcal{S}} such that each element in 𝒳 \mathcal{X} is contained in exactly one subset of 𝒮 ∗ \mathcal{S}^{\ast} . This concept becomes clearer when we rename elements in 𝒳 \mathcal{X} to items and 𝒮 \mathcal{S} to options . We want to find the subcollection 𝒮 ∗ \mathcal{S}^{*} of options to cover all items exactly once. One example comes from Knuth (2020) : Let 𝒳 = { a , b , c , d , e , f , g } \mathcal{X}=\{a,b,c,d,e,f,g\} be items and the collection of options 𝒮 = { [ c , e ] , [ a , d , g ] , [ b , c , f ] , [ a , d , f ] , [ b , g ] , [ d , e , g ] } \mathcal{S}=\{{\bigl[c,e\bigr],\bigl[a,d,g\bigr],\bigl[b,c,f\bigr],\bigl[a,d,f\bigr],\bigl[b,g\bigr],\bigl[d,e,g\bigr]}\} . When selecting the first, fourth, and fifth options, we cover each item exactly once, i.e. 𝒮 ∗ = { [ c , e ] , [ a , d , f ] , [ b , g ] } \mathcal{S}^{\ast}=\{\bigl[c,e\bigr],\bigl[a,d,f\bigr],\bigl[b,g\bigr]\} . This is very useful, as such exact-1 properties have a large variety of encodings with strong performance impacts for solvers, as discussed in the context of SAT-solving in Nguyen et al. (2020) . Colored Exact Cover. Exact cover can be extended by splitting the options into primary items 𝒳 P \mathcal{X}_{P} and secondary items 𝒳 S \mathcal{X}_{S} such that 𝒳 = 𝒳 P ∪ 𝒳 S \mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_{P}\cup\mathcal{X}_{S} . Let ℰ \mathcal{E} denote a set of colors that can be used to color (change) secondary items. Now, each primary item must still be covered exactly once , while secondary items must be assigned at most one color. Note that colors can be shared between options, i.e. multiple options with secondary items of matching colors may be selected. Notation. We write options as sets of comma-separated items enclosed in brackets, e.g., [ a , b ] \bigl[a,b\bigr] . We use colons to separate secondary items and colors. Thus, a : c a:c means the secondary item a ∈ 𝒳 S a\in\mathcal{X}_{S} has the color c ∈ ℰ c\in\mathcal{E} . Items may be combined from other terms using angle brackets, e.g. ⟨ a , b ⟩ \langle{}a,b\rangle{} is one item. For instance, [ ⟨ a , b ⟩ : 1 , c ] \bigl[\langle{}a,b\rangle{}:{}1,c\bigr] denotes an option of one item ⟨ a , b ⟩ \langle{}a,b\rangle{} with the color 1 1 (meaning ⟨ a , b ⟩ \langle{}a,b\rangle{} must be a secondary item), and c c as another item. A set of options is enclosed in curly brackets. MiniExact . It is an efficient implementation 2 2 2 https://github.com/miniexact/miniexact of some of the Dancing Links algorithms of Knuth (2020) . Its performance mostly mirrors Knuth’s original C implementation, while also offering a user-friendly Python API and a more sophisticated parser. The algorithm can be selected at run-time, making it a useful tool for experiments with exact cover problems. 2.2 Zebra Puzzles Zebra Puzzles are classic constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) where a solver must find a one-to-one mapping across entity categories using logical clues (see Fig. 1 ). Formulation. Each puzzle consists of initial statements defining a finite set of entities ℰ = { e 1 , … , e N } \mathcal{E}=\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{N}\} (e.g., numbered houses) with N > 1 N>1 ; several characteristics or properties 𝒫 = { p 1 , … , p M } \mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{M}\} (e.g., name, car, animal) with M ≥ 1 M\geq 1 , each containing N N mutually exclusive attributes; and a set of clues 𝒞 = { c 1 , … , c K } \mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{K}\} with K ≥ 1 K\geq 1 that relate entities, properties, and attributes. All attributes of a property define its domain 𝒜 p = { a p ​ 1 , … , a p ​ N } \mathcal{A}_{p}=\{a_{p1},\ldots,a_{pN}\} (e.g., cat, horse) with | 𝒜 p | = N |\mathcal{A}_{p}|=N . Constraints. To ensure uniqueness of each puzzle’s solution, uniqueness and clue-based constraints have to be fulfilled. The uniqueness constraint ensures that every attribute a ∈ 𝒜 p a\in\mathcal{A}_{p} is assigned exactly to one entity for all p ∈ 𝒫 p\in\mathcal{P} . Clue-based constraints formalize the different verbal clues into logic statements that must be satisfied by a valid solution. For Zebra Puzzles, there are 8 different clue-based constraints that relate attributes and/or entities by specifying presence/absence or positional relations as summarized in Appx. A.3 . Task. The goal is to find an assignment x p , e ∈ 𝒜 p x_{p,e}\in\mathcal{A}_{p} selecting an attribute for each property p ∈ 𝒫 p\in\mathcal{P} and entity e ∈ ℰ e\in\mathcal{E} such that all constraints are fulfilled. Note that these assignments can be summarized into a tabular grid where the columns are defined by the entities, the rows by the properties, and the assigned attributes are listed in the corresponding cells. Datasets. Zebra Puzzles are used as proxies to test the reasoning capabilities of modern LLMs ( Lin et al., 2025 ; White et al., 2025 ) . To this end, Lin et al. (2025) introduced the ZebraLogic dataset containing 1,000 logic grid puzzles of various sizes ( N × M N\times M ) ranging from 2 × 2 2\times 2 to 6 × 6 6\times 6 . We extend this dataset to include 400 bigger puzzle instances ( 7 × 5 7\times 5 , … \ldots , 8 × 10 8\times 10 ) and call this extended dataset ZebraExtreme 3 3 3 Data is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/pskaisg/ZebraExtreme . . Following Lin et al. (2025) , we partition the puzzles according to their solution space size ( | 𝒬 | = ( N ! ) M |\mathcal{Q}|=(N!)^{M} ) into bins: S \displaystyle\mathrm{S} : 10 0 ≤ | 𝒬 | < 10 3 , \displaystyle\colon\;10^{0}\leq|\mathcal{Q}|<10^{3}, M \displaystyle\mathrm{M} : 10 3 ≤ | 𝒬 | < 10 6 , \displaystyle\colon\;10^{3}\leq|\mathcal{Q}|<10^{6}, L \displaystyle\mathrm{L} : 10 6 ≤ | 𝒬 | < 10 10 , \displaystyle\colon\;10^{6}\leq|\mathcal{Q}|<10^{10}, XL \displaystyle\mathrm{XL} : 10 10 ≤ | 𝒬 | < 10 18 , \displaystyle\colon\;10^{10}\leq|\mathcal{Q}|<10^{18}, XXL \displaystyle\mathrm{XXL} : 10 18 ≤ | 𝒬 | < 10 30 , \displaystyle\colon\;10^{18}\leq|\mathcal{Q}|<10^{30}, XXXL \displaystyle\mathrm{XXXL} : 10 30 ≤ | 𝒬 | < 10 50 . \displaystyle\colon\;10^{30}\leq|\mathcal{Q}|<10^{50}. Note that the bins S to XL are included in the original ZebraLogic dataset, while the ZebraExtreme only includes puzzles in XXL and XXXL. Appx. A.2 describes how we created this computationally challenging dataset. 3 Solving Zebra Puzzles with Exact Cover In the following, we present NeuralExactCover , a neural-symbolic approach for solving Zebra logic puzzles. As in Figure 1 , we leverage the in-context learning capabilities of LLMs to extract semantic relations between entities, properties, and attributes from free-text puzzle descriptions and translate them into an exact cover encoding. The symbolic module then computes solutions and provides feedback on the resulting encoding, allowing the LLM to iteratively refine its tool calls until a unique solution is obtained. This feedback loop integrates neural language understanding with symbolic reasoning. 3.1 Language Module for Puzzle Parsing The main goal of the language module is the conversion of the problem from natural language to a valid exact cover encoding. At the core of this module is a language model. To this end, we consider several recent open weight LLMs that are state-of-the-art for their parameter size, such as Qwen3 ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , gpt-oss ( OpenAI et al., 2025 ) , Magistral ( Rastogi et al., 2025a ) , and Devstral ( Rastogi et al., 2025b ) . Note that any language model that has been fine-tuned to perform tool calling could be used. The model is prompted to complete the following sequence of actions: harmonization , clue extraction and formalization . The full prompt is listed in Appx. A.4 . It includes manually constructed few-shot examples to improve the adherence of the model to the specific instructions given. Harmonization. First, each puzzle is paraphrased such that every attribute occurrence follows the format < < property-name > > @ < < attribute-name > > . This reduces ambiguity arising from attributes that occur under multiple properties. For example, if “cat” is used by two different properties, it may be extracted incorrectly, resulting in an erroneous encoding. Clue extraction. First, the LLM parses the puzzle’s setup (i.e. M M , N N , { 𝒜 p } p ∈ 𝒫 \{\mathcal{A}_{p}\}_{p\in\mathcal{P}} , and K K ) and proceeds to extract the clues. The model is instructed to use our exact cover encoding’s tool-calls presented in the next section to express the extracted clues. Consequently, the output of the LLM is a list of tool calls in JSON format, specifying the called function and its arguments. D ). 3.2 Reasoning Module using Exact Cover We use exact cover as a logic backbone since it natively expresses exact-one constraints instead of requiring complex encodings as in SAT-solving and solvers naturally support enumerating solutions without employing blocking clauses ( Nguyen et al., 2020 ) . Items. We assign a primary item to all clues 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , ensuring that each must be used once. We implement the proposed exact cover encoding using the MiniExact Python API. The encoding is exposed through a set of documented functions corresponding to the clue types in Appx. A.3 , enabling LLMs to construct exact cover instances via tool calls. First, the generated tool calls are checked for completeness by verifying that tool calls were produced and that their number matches the number of puzzle clues. If tool calls are missing or excessive, the LLM is prompted to generate one tool call per clue, add missing clue encodings, or re-evaluate redundant or conflicting ones. If the number of tool calls and parsed clues matches, the corresponding encoding is evaluated by the MiniExact solver. For feedback, the following three outcomes are considered: Overconstrained If no solution exists, the generated constraints are overconstraining, indicating an error in clue extraction. The LLM receives symbolic feedback and is instructed to revise at least one previous tool call to make the encoding less restrictive. Underconstrained If multiple solutions are found, the encoding is underconstrained, and the LLM is prompted to revise its clue interpretations by modifying at least one tool call. Unique solution If a unique solution is found, the encoding is considered sufficiently complete and consistent, and the solution is returned. The corresponding prompts and additional details are listed in Appx. A.6 . 4 Experiments We evaluate the reasoning performance of plain LLMs (without tools), Logic-LM ( Pan et al., 2023 ) , Logic.py ( Kesseli et al., 2025 ) , and our NeuralExactCover (NEC) in a LLM model agnostic way on Zebra Puzzles. To apply Logic-LM to these logic puzzles, we extended its CSP pipeline by adding a Zebra puzzle specific prompt and adapting the solution parsing, see Appx B.2 . Note that Logic.py implements a feedback mechanism to correct for syntax errors and UNSAT encodings. For numerical evaluation, we consider the recent ZebraLogic benchmark ( Lin et al., 2025 ) and our introduced ZebraExtreme, a more challenging variant characterized by a larger number of cells and an expanded set of possible values per cell. Refer to Appx A.2 for details on this dataset. To assess the reasoning and scaling capabilities of the different methods, we evaluate puzzle and cell accuracy. While the former counts the fraction of correctly solved puzzles, the latter counts the fraction of correctly assigned attributes to entities (i.e. cells in the solution table). In addition, we evaluate the runtime of the LLMs and the symbolic solvers. We stratify the runtime and puzzle accuracy by the puzzle size into bins S to XXXL to analyze how models perform on increasingly complex puzzles. For all methods, each LLM was run with temperature set to 0 0 and top_p set to 1 1 following Lin et al. (2025) . We also adopt an output token budget of 4096 per LLM call, except for ZebraExtreme, where the budget is increased to 30720 to accommodate reasoning over larger puzzles. Notably, Logic.py Lin et al. (2025) employs a multi-step LLM pipeline checking for syntax and constraint-encoding errors at each stage and reruns LLMs when such errors occur, thereby enabling multiple self-correction attempts. Since all four approaches under consideration are LLM-agnostic, we evaluate LLMs across a diverse range of parameter scales, training paradigms, and families. items.raw_text: From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles Thanks: Equal supervision Equal contribution Paulius Skaisgiris Email: paulius.skaisgiris@tuwien.ac.at Affiliation: Institute of Logic and Computation, TU Wien, Austria 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Institute for Application-Oriented Knowledge Processing, JKU Linz, Austria Department of Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity, University of Klagenfurt, Austria Institute for Machine Learning, JKU Linz, Austria Institute for Symbolic Artificial Intelligence, JKU Linz, Austria 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Institute for Machine Learning, LIT AI Lab, Department of Virtual Morphology, Clinical Research Institute Medical AI, JKU Linz, Austria Thomas Pammer Email: tpammer@faw.jku.at Affiliation: Veronika Semmelrock Email: veronika.semmelrock@aau.at Affiliation: Mykyta Ielanskyi Email: ielanskyi@ml.jku.at Affiliation: Maximilian Heisinger Email: maximilian.heisinger@jku.at Affiliation: Erich Kobler Email: erich.kobler@jku.at Affiliation: Abstract Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation has substantially improved the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, including code generation, data analysis, and exam-style question answering. Despite these advances, purely neural LLMs continue to struggle with elementary logical reasoning problems and lack the determinism, soundness, and reliability characteristic of symbolic reasoning systems. Conversely, classical symbolic methods such as SAT solving and exact cover guarantee correctness and completeness, but require problems to be expressed in highly specialized formal encodings, limiting their applicability to natural language inputs. In this work, we present a synergistic neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by combining neural semantic parsing with deterministic exact cover reasoning. Given a Zebra-style logic puzzle in natural language, an LLM translates entities and constraints into structured tool calls that construct an exact cover instance. A symbolic solver then computes the solution and provides feedback to iteratively refine invalid, under- or overconstrained encodings, exploiting the uniqueness property of Zebra puzzles. We conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple parameter scales, post-training paradigms, and LLM families. The results demonstrate that our hybrid approach consistently outperforms strong plain neural baselines, including CoT prompting, as well as recent neuro-symbolic methods. 1 1 1 Code is available at https://codeberg.org/bilai-ss25-booleguru-llm/zebrallm . 1 Introduction Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs) lie at the core of many real-world decision-making tasks, including scheduling, planning, resource allocation, and configuration, making them a fundamental abstraction in AI research ( Russell and Norvig, 1995 ; Mackworth, 1977 ; Nadel, 1989 ; Knuth, 2016 ; Knuth, 2020 ; Knuth, 2025 ) . While symbolic methods such as SAT and constraint solvers can guarantee correctness and completeness, their practical deployment critically depends on constructing effective formal encodings – a process that remains difficult even for domain experts ( Heisinger et al., 2024 ) . Translating informal problem descriptions into a structured encoding requires substantial modeling expertise as small representational choices can dramatically impact solver performance and tractability. As a result, research often studies simplified yet representative proxy domains such as logic puzzles (e.g. Sudoku or Zebra Puzzles), which capture essential combinatorial and relational reasoning challenges while providing clean semantics, controllable complexity, and objectively verifiable solutions ( Dechter and Pearl, 1987 ; Prosser, 1993 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; White et al., 2025 ) . This reliance on structured benchmark domains aligns naturally with recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), which are increasingly applied to tasks requiring the construction of structured symbolic solutions from unstructured inputs. Such domains include mathematical reasoning ( Hendrycks et al., 2021b ) , programming ( Hendrycks et al., 2021a ) , planning ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and logic puzzle solving ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Chollet et al., 2025 ) . A shared characteristic of these problems is that, although discovering solutions is challenging, their correctness can be verified algorithmically. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards post-training has therefore emerged as a standard approach for optimizing models directly against symbolic verifiers ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . The resulting thinking LLMs produce Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning traces enabling inference-time scaling. Figure 1: Visualization of NeuralExactCover . A puzzle instance is combined with our prompt template and processed by an LLM that harmonizes attributes, extracts entities and clues, and translates clues into an exact cover encoding. The symbolic MiniExact solver then solves the encoding and provides iterative feedback on failures to refine the generated tool calls. This loop continues until a unique solution is found or the retry limit is reached, after which the solution is converted into plain text. Zebra Puzzles are among recent benchmarks to test the reasoning capabilities of LLMs ( Lin et al., 2025 ; White et al., 2025 ) . They consist of lists of entities, properties, and attributes as well as clues; the goal is to infer the relations of attributes and entities from the given information. Lin et al. (2025) find that scaling the model size does not help beyond a certain level of complexity which is defined by the puzzles’ solution space. This manifests in generalist LLMs faring extremely well on simple Zebra Puzzles while struggling with more complex ones. Longer reasoning traces appear to be more helpful with these problems than larger models. However, these longer traces present additional challenges such as high frequency noise ( Radler et al., 2025 ) and increased chance of hallucination ( Mei et al., 2025 ) . To address the reasoning limitations of purely neural models, recent neuro-symbolic approaches increasingly combine LLM-based semantic parsing with symbolic solvers to enforce logical consistency ( Dinu et al., 2024 ) . Prior work explores both agentic formulations that iteratively generate solver-compatible programs and solver-centric pipelines that translate natural language inputs into formal constraint specifications solved using SAT, SMT, CSP, or ASP techniques ( Szeider, 2025 ; Pan et al., 2023 ; Ye et al., 2023 ; Eiter et al., 2025 ) . Notably, Logic.py ( Kesseli et al., 2025 ) translates natural language into a domain-specific representation solved by an exact constraint solver, incorporating iterative error feedback to the LLM. This coupling of semantic parsing and symbolic solving consistently outperforms LLMs on Zebra Puzzle-style benchmarks. In this work, we present an integrated neuro-symbolic framework called NeuralExactCover that combines LLM-based semantic parsing with deterministic exact cover solving for reliable logical reasoning over plain text Zebra-style puzzles. Our main contributions are as follows: • We introduce and adapt an exact cover encoding for efficient symbolic solving of Zebra-style logic puzzles. • We introduce a neuro-symbolic framework that leverages LLMs as a translation layer for an exact cover solver and re-applies symbolic results as feedback to the LLM. • We introduce the ZebraExtreme dataset, extending ZebraLogic ( Lin et al., 2025 ) with even more challenging problems of size up to 8 × 10 8\times 10 entities and properties. 2 Background and Preliminaries 2.1 Exact Cover Given a collection S S of subsets of a set 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , the exact cover problem is about finding a subcollection 𝒮 ∗ ⊆ 𝒮 \mathcal{S}^{*}\subseteq{\mathcal{S}} such that each element in 𝒳 \mathcal{X} is contained in exactly one subset of 𝒮 ∗ \mathcal{S}^{\ast} . This concept becomes clearer when we rename elements in 𝒳 \mathcal{X} to items and 𝒮 \mathcal{S} to options . We want to find the subcollection 𝒮 ∗ \mathcal{S}^{*} of options to cover all items exactly once. One example comes from Knuth (2020) : Let 𝒳 = { a , b , c , d , e , f , g } \mathcal{X}=\{a,b,c,d,e,f,g\} be items and the collection of options 𝒮 = { [ c , e ] , [ a , d , g ] , [ b , c , f ] , [ a , d , f ] , [ b , g ] , [ d , e , g ] } \mathcal{S}=\{{\bigl[c,e\bigr],\bigl[a,d,g\bigr],\bigl[b,c,f\bigr],\bigl[a,d,f\bigr],\bigl[b,g\bigr],\bigl[d,e,g\bigr]}\} . When selecting the first, fourth, and fifth options, we cover each item exactly once, i.e. 𝒮 ∗ = { [ c , e ] , [ a , d , f ] , [ b , g ] } \mathcal{S}^{\ast}=\{\bigl[c,e\bigr],\bigl[a,d,f\bigr],\bigl[b,g\bigr]\} . This is very useful, as such exact-1 properties have a large variety of encodings with strong performance impacts for solvers, as discussed in the context of SAT-solving in Nguyen et al. (2020) . Colored Exact Cover. Exact cover can be extended by splitting the options into primary items 𝒳 P \mathcal{X}_{P} and secondary items 𝒳 S \mathcal{X}_{S} such that 𝒳 = 𝒳 P ∪ 𝒳 S \mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_{P}\cup\mathcal{X}_{S} . Let ℰ \mathcal{E} denote a set of colors that can be used to color (change) secondary items. Now, each primary item must still be covered exactly once , while secondary items must be assigned at most one color. Note that colors can be shared between options, i.e. multiple options with secondary items of matching colors may be selected. Notation. We write options as sets of comma-separated items enclosed in brackets, e.g., [ a , b ] \bigl[a,b\bigr] . We use colons to separate secondary items and colors. Thus, a : c a:c means the secondary item a ∈ 𝒳 S a\in\mathcal{X}_{S} has the color c ∈ ℰ c\in\mathcal{E} . Items may be combined from other terms using angle brackets, e.g. ⟨ a , b ⟩ \langle{}a,b\rangle{} is one item. For instance, [ ⟨ a , b ⟩ : 1 , c ] \bigl[\langle{}a,b\rangle{}:{}1,c\bigr] denotes an option of one item ⟨ a , b ⟩ \langle{}a,b\rangle{} with the color 1 1 (meaning ⟨ a , b ⟩ \langle{}a,b\rangle{} must be a secondary item), and c c as another item. A set of options is enclosed in curly brackets. MiniExact . It is an efficient implementation 2 2 2 https://github.com/miniexact/miniexact of some of the Dancing Links algorithms of Knuth (2020) . Its performance mostly mirrors Knuth’s original C implementation, while also offering a user-friendly Python API and a more sophisticated parser. The algorithm can be selected at run-time, making it a useful tool for experiments with exact cover problems. 2.2 Zebra Puzzles Zebra Puzzles are classic constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) where a solver must find a one-to-one mapping across entity categories using logical clues (see Fig. 1 ). Formulation. Each puzzle consists of initial statements defining a finite set of entities ℰ = { e 1 , … , e N } \mathcal{E}=\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{N}\} (e.g., numbered houses) with N > 1 N>1 ; several characteristics or properties 𝒫 = { p 1 , … , p M } \mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{M}\} (e.g., name, car, animal) with M ≥ 1 M\geq 1 , each containing N N mutually exclusive attributes; and a set of clues 𝒞 = { c 1 , … , c K } \mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{K}\} with K ≥ 1 K\geq 1 that relate entities, properties, and attributes. All attributes of a property define its domain 𝒜 p = { a p ​ 1 , … , a p ​ N } \mathcal{A}_{p}=\{a_{p1},\ldots,a_{pN}\} (e.g., cat, horse) with | 𝒜 p | = N |\mathcal{A}_{p}|=N . Constraints. To ensure uniqueness of each puzzle’s solution, uniqueness and clue-based constraints have to be fulfilled. The uniqueness constraint ensures that every attribute a ∈ 𝒜 p a\in\mathcal{A}_{p} is assigned exactly to one entity for all p ∈ 𝒫 p\in\mathcal{P} . Clue-based constraints formalize the different verbal clues into logic statements that must be satisfied by a valid solution. For Zebra Puzzles, there are 8 different clue-based constraints that relate attributes and/or entities by specifying presence/absence or positional relations as summarized in Appx. A.3 . Task. The goal is to find an assignment x p , e ∈ 𝒜 p x_{p,e}\in\mathcal{A}_{p} selecting an attribute for each property p ∈ 𝒫 p\in\mathcal{P} and entity e ∈ ℰ e\in\mathcal{E} such that all constraints are fulfilled. Note that these assignments can be summarized into a tabular grid where the columns are defined by the entities, the rows by the properties, and the assigned attributes are listed in the corresponding cells. Datasets. Zebra Puzzles are used as proxies to test the reasoning capabilities of modern LLMs ( Lin et al., 2025 ; White et al., 2025 ) . To this end, Lin et al. (2025) introduced the ZebraLogic dataset containing 1,000 logic grid puzzles of various sizes ( N × M N\times M ) ranging from 2 × 2 2\times 2 to 6 × 6 6\times 6 . We extend this dataset to include 400 bigger puzzle instances ( 7 × 5 7\times 5 , … \ldots , 8 × 10 8\times 10 ) and call this extended dataset ZebraExtreme 3 3 3 Data is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/pskaisg/ZebraExtreme . . Following Lin et al. As in Figure 1 , we leverage the in-context learning capabilities of LLMs to extract semantic relations between entities, properties, and attributes from free-text puzzle descriptions and translate them into an exact cover encoding. The symbolic module then computes solutions and provides feedback on the resulting encoding, allowing the LLM to iteratively refine its tool calls until a unique solution is obtained. This feedback loop integrates neural language understanding with symbolic reasoning. 3.1 Language Module for Puzzle Parsing The main goal of the language module is the conversion of the problem from natural language to a valid exact cover encoding. At the core of this module is a language model. To this end, we consider several recent open weight LLMs that are state-of-the-art for their parameter size, such as Qwen3 ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , gpt-oss ( OpenAI et al., 2025 ) , Magistral ( Rastogi et al., 2025a ) , and Devstral ( Rastogi et al., 2025b ) . For all methods, each LLM was run with temperature set to 0 0 and top_p set to 1 1 following Lin et al. (2025) . We also adopt an output token budget of 4096 per LLM call, except for ZebraExtreme, where the budget is increased to 30720 to accommodate reasoning over larger puzzles. Notably, Logic.py Lin et al. (2025) employs a multi-step LLM pipeline checking for syntax and constraint-encoding errors at each stage and reruns LLMs when such errors occur, thereby enabling multiple self-correction attempts. Consequently, the total token usage may exceed the output token budget of 4096. In contrast, our approach relies on a single LLM call. Further details on models and serving are in Appx A.1 . Since all four approaches under consideration are LLM-agnostic, we evaluate LLMs across a diverse range of parameter scales, training paradigms, and families. items.content: Algorithms and theory Google’s mission presents many exciting algorithmic and optimization challenges across different product areas including Search, Ads, Social, and Google Infrastructure. These include optimizing internal systems such as scheduling the machines that power the numerous computations done each day, as well as optimizations that affect core products and users, from online allocation of ads to page-views to automatic management of ad campaigns, and from clustering large-scale graphs to finding best paths in transportation networks. Other than employing new algorithmic ideas to impact millions of users, Google researchers contribute to the state-of-the-art research in these areas by publishing in top conferences and journals. Recent Publications See More Depth-CoT Tradeoffs in Transformers: A Look at Path Following Clayton Sanford Matus Telgarsky Justin D. Li 2027 Preview Preview abstract Modern transformers have been scaled up in size, data, training-time compute, and more recently test-time compute based on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the consequences of trading off these parameters are unknown. We construct explicit tradeoffs between two of these aspects: the number of layers in a transformer and the number of CoT tokens. Our first result is general: with mild assumptions and a single-token prompt, for any integer k, a transformer using soft attention and SwiGLU MLP layers with L layers and n CoT tokens can be converted to a transformer with at most ckL layers and ⌈n/k⌉ CoT tokens, and vice versa, although with an increase to the size of other parameters. We then a multi-token prompt path following task, finding that additional preprocessing from the multi-token prompt changes the depth-CoT relationship in this case. We construct an attention-only network with L layers and 2^(L−2) heads that can traverse 2^(L−1) − 1 edges along a path with a single CoT token, demonstrating at least an exponential relationship between increases in depth and reductions in the number of CoT tokens needed to traverse the entire path. This relationship for the path following task holds empirically as well, as demonstrated by training networks with up to 5 layers, with the tradeoff between depth and the maximum number of edge traversals in a single CoT token exactly matching our theoretical constructions. View details Surviving the perfect storm: how hardware PMs can beat the AI tax and trade tariffs Akash Rathi Mind The Product (2026) Preview Preview abstract This piece analyzes how hardware product managers can navigate the financial pressure of AI-related costs and trade tariffs. It presents a practical framework for deploying the Joint Development Model (JDM) as a product development strategy to balance innovation with cost efficiency, enabling sustainable growth for next-generation AI-native consumer devices. View details Marginalized Bundle Adjustment: Multi-View Camera Pose from Monocular Depth Estimates Shengjie Zhu Ahmed Abdelkader Mark Matthews Xiaoming Liu Vincent Chu International Conference on 3D Vision (2026) Preview Preview abstract Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a classical 3D vision task for recovering camera parameters and scene geometry from multi-view images. Recent advances in deep learning enable accurate monocular depth estimation (MDE) that infers structure from a single image without depending on camera motion. But integrating MDE into SfM remains challenging. Unlike classical triangulated sparse pointclouds, MDE produces dense depthmaps with significantly higher error variance. Inspired by modern RANSAC estimators, we propose a Marginalized Bundle Adjustment (MBA) to accommodate MDE error variance with its density. With MBA, we show that MDE depthmaps are sufficiently accurate to support SoTA or competitive results in Structure-from-Motion and camera relocalization. Our benchmark demonstrates consistent remarkable results from two-view, few-frames small multiview, to thousands-frames large multiview system. Our method highlights the significant potential of MDE on multi-view 3D vision tasks. View details Cardio Load in exercise and everyday life: A modified TRIMP metric for continuously-sensing consumer wearables Justin Phillips Daniel Roggen YongSuk Cho Robert Harle Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise (2026) Preview Preview abstract PURPOSE: To introduce Cardio Load (CL), a metric quantifying cardiovascular work from all activities across the day, and to investigate its distribution by age, gender, and workout profiles. CL adapts the Training Impulse (TRIMP) model by leveraging continuous heart rate and movement data from wearables, enabling minute-level intensity estimation. We also discuss the derivation of weekly target loads, intended to guide fitness maintenance. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 31.2 million hours of wrist-worn wearable data collected over a six-week period. The dataset comprised a 40,000-subject subset (37.9% female) of consenting Google Pixel Watch® users in the United States, aged 18 to 80 years (18-39: 41.8%, 40-59: 43.5%, 60+: 14.6%). Measured data included minute-interval heart rate averages, resting and maximum heart rates, minute-interval averaged accelerometer log energy, and manually-logged or auto-detected activity types. Cardio Load scores and target loads were calculated daily for each subject and compared across age and gender. We also compared the proportions of CL gained during workouts and incidental daily activities for these groups. RESULTS: Overall, the study population's mean ± SD weekly CL scores were 221 ± 156 (female) and 259 ± 169 (male). Median weekly Cardio Load (CL) values exhibited consistency for individuals between 30 and 75 years of age. When analyzed in five-year age groups, the coefficient of variation (CV%) of median weekly CL values within this age range was less than 4.5%, with younger and older subjects demonstrating higher and lower median CL, respectively. The median proportion of CL accumulated during structured workouts versus incidental daily activity was 41.0% (female) and 49.0% (male) for all subjects, though this varied considerably with average weekly workout duration. CV% of weekly target load and daily target load over 6 weeks was 23.6% and 35.2% respectively. The machine has been derived automatically from a higher-order evaluator that uses the technique of memothunks to implement laziness. The derivation has been done with the use of an off-the-shelf transformation tool implementing the "functional correspondence" between higher-order interpreters and abstract machines, and it yields a simple and concise description of the machine. We prove that the resulting machine conservatively extends the lazy version of Krivine machine for the weak call-by-need strategy, and that it simulates the normal-order strategy in bilinear number of steps. View details Geo-Contextual AI Concierge: Minimizing Internal Support Friction Through Proactive Knowledge Synthesis Neeraj Choudhary Dónal Doyle Technical Report (2026) Preview Preview abstract In large-scale distributed enterprises, traditional Knowledge Management (KM) systems face a critical failure mode: static documentation cannot keep pace with evolving operational realities and regional nuances. This "knowledge latency" forces employees out of self-service workflows and into costly support ticketing queues. This paper introduces SENTINEL, a geo-contextual AI framework designed to shift enterprise support from reactive retrieval to proactive interception. The architecture employs a novel dual-engine system integrated into an omni-present interface. The first engine utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct pre-emptive, historical case-grounded audits of documentation, generating a "Contextual Density" score that identifies friction zones. The second engine is an autonomous Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) agent that surfaces in-situ via a location-intelligent assistant window, resolving queries in real-time. By functioning as a strategic "defensive barrier" at the point of origin, SENTINEL demonstrates how a proactive AI assistant can drive high-fidelity, in-situ case deflection. These include optimizing internal systems such as scheduling the machines that power the numerous computations done each day, as well as optimizations that affect core products and users, from online allocation of ads to page-views to automatic management of ad campaigns, and from clustering large-scale graphs to finding best paths in transportation networks. Recent Publications See More Depth-CoT Tradeoffs in Transformers: A Look at Path Following Clayton Sanford Matus Telgarsky Justin D. Li 2027 Preview Preview abstract Modern transformers have been scaled up in size, data, training-time compute, and more recently test-time compute based on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the consequences of trading off these parameters are unknown. We construct explicit tradeoffs between two of these aspects: the number of layers in a transformer and the number of CoT tokens. Our first result is general: with mild assumptions and a single-token prompt, for any integer k, a transformer using soft attention and SwiGLU MLP layers with L layers and n CoT tokens can be converted to a transformer with at most ckL layers and ⌈n/k⌉ CoT tokens, and vice versa, although with an increase to the size of other parameters. We then a multi-token prompt path following task, finding that additional preprocessing from the multi-token prompt changes the depth-CoT relationship in this case. We construct an attention-only network with L layers and 2^(L−2) heads that can traverse 2^(L−1) − 1 edges along a path with a single CoT token, demonstrating at least an exponential relationship between increases in depth and reductions in the number of CoT tokens needed to traverse the entire path. This relationship for the path following task holds empirically as well, as demonstrated by training networks with up to 5 layers, with the tradeoff between depth and the maximum number of edge traversals in a single CoT token exactly matching our theoretical constructions. items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans.
