items.raw_text: Back to Articles Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3 Team Article Published October 27, 2026 Upvote 97 +91 Leonie Monigatti iamleonie Follow LiquidAI Jimmy T.H. Smith jimmysmith1919 Follow LiquidAI Anthony Maltsev amaltsev Follow LiquidAI Maxime Labonne mlabonne Follow LiquidAI Brandon Brandon3967 Follow LiquidAI Samuel Stevens samuelstevens Follow LiquidAI Ryan Shubert shubeydoo Follow LiquidAI Tianshu Yu tianshu-yu Follow LiquidAI Sina s-jse Follow LiquidAI Tim Seyde tseyde Follow LiquidAI Rouzbeh Amin Tafreshi rouzbehat78 Follow LiquidAI Alexander Amini alexanderamini Follow LiquidAI Saniya Karwa saniyakarwa Follow LiquidAI Marc Harkonen haerski Follow LiquidAI Anna Piunova orech Follow LiquidAI Calder Katyal CalderKat Follow LiquidAI Ishwarya Ananthabhotla ianant93 Follow LiquidAI Farris Atif farris-liquid Follow LiquidAI Tarek Dakhran tdakhran Follow LiquidAI Paul Pak paulpak58 Follow LiquidAI xx tugot17 Follow LiquidAI Mihir Bafna mihirbafna Follow LiquidAI Kyle Bruce Wheeler m3m0ryh0l3 Follow LiquidAI Aditya Tadimeti adityatadimeti Follow LiquidAI Alfred Eng alfredeng Follow LiquidAI Karthik Macherla karthikrmacherla Follow LiquidAI Khoi Nguyen KTLK Follow LiquidAI Aldo Gael Carranza agcarranza Follow LiquidAI Aurelien Lac Aurelien-Lac Follow LiquidAI Tyler Murray undfined Follow LiquidAI Raahul Vignesh Raahul26 Follow LiquidAI Song Duong sduong Follow LiquidAI Ramin Hasani raminmh Follow LiquidAI Mathias Lechner mlech26l Follow LiquidAI Akhilesh Deepak Gotmare akhileshdeepakgotmare Follow LiquidAI Fernando Fernandes Neto fernandofernandes Follow LiquidAI Jiahui Wang WWWjiahui Follow LiquidAI Yuri Khrustalev ykhrustalev Follow LiquidAI Alay Shah alay2shah Follow LiquidAI Simon Lee yungisimon Follow LiquidAI Mayank Agarwal mayankagarwal Follow LiquidAI Zetian Li zetianli Follow LiquidAI changyi yang changyiyang Follow LiquidAI Sinoué GAD GAD-cell Follow LiquidAI nathan ranchin nathanrchn Follow LiquidAI Sergei Tilga tilgasergey Follow LiquidAI LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs. LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family: More capability per parameter: a new tri-hybrid architecture and training recipe allow LFM3-1.7B to outperform LFM2.5-2.6B while using 35% fewer parameters. Every modality on one backbone: six 2B-class models (text, vision, audio, omni, and decision) trained from LFM3-1.7B-Base, including our first omni model and video input for our vision model. Built for the edge: the text model fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit precision, new in-house vision and audio encoders speed up processing, and the text model’s 256K context window lets agents run on-device. Made to be specialized: every model fine-tunes on a single GPU, so you can adapt it to your data, terminology, and deployment environment. How we built a more expressive backbone LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes: Tri-hybrid layer mix: 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention (SWA) layers with a 256-token window, and 6 global attention layers. The convolutions use a kernel size of 7, up from 3 in LFM2. Head-wise gated attention: a sigmoid gate scales each head's output, so a head can switch off when it has nothing to add. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization. Partial RoPE: global attention layers rotate only the highest-frequency half of each head, so the other half matches on content regardless of distance. SWA layers keep full RoPE. Sandwich norm: each block normalizes both its input and its output to keep activations well-scaled. The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B . The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens. One backbone for six models Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device. Model Input Output Built on LFM3-1.7B Text Text LFM3-1.7B-Base LFM3-VL-2B Text, images, video Text LFM3 backbone + vision encoder LFM3-Audio-2B Text, audio Text, speech LFM3 backbone + audio encoder, audio decoder, and LiquidCodec LFM3-Omni-2B Text, images, video, audio Text, speech LFM3 backbone + vision and audio encoders and audio decoder d1-2B Text, images, video Calibrated answers LFM3-VL-2B d1-omni-2B Text, images, video, audio Calibrated answers LFM3-Omni-2B The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders: Vision encoder: it combines convolution and attention and uses 3x less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models. Our 164M-parameter encoder matches Qwen3.5-2B's vision encoder in accuracy while requiring 2.2x fewer FLOPs (both measured with the same LFM2.5-230M language backbone). For video, it embeds each pair of sampled frames into one temporal slice, halving the temporal sequence length. Audio encoder and LiquidCodec: the audio encoder mixes sliding-window attention and short convolutions and is fully causal, so the model can prefill while you speak, with time to first token as low as 50 ms. LiquidCodec, our new audio tokenizer, turns generated tokens into speech at about 87x real time on a single CPU thread on Apple M4 Max and supports streaming decoding. How to use the LFM3 models Each model runs in transformers . The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports. LFM3-1.7B Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card . To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers : pip install -U transformers Then load and run the model: from transformers import pipeline generator = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B" , trust_remote_code= True , ) messages = [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is C. elegans?" }] output = generator( messages, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.1 , max_new_tokens= 2048 , ) print (output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ][ "content" ]) For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide . LFM3-VL-2B Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card . To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.21.0" torch torchvision pillow Then load and run the model: import torch from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B" model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map= "auto" , trust_remote_code= True ) processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "url" : "https://placecats.com/300/200" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Describe this image." }, ], } ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.1 , max_new_tokens= 16384 , # generate() needs an explicit limit; reasoning can be long ) generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] print (processor.batch_decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens= True )[ 0 ]) See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp. LFM3-Audio-2B Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card . To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch accelerate librosa soundfile Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub: import torch import soundfile as sf from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B" device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32 model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code= True ). eval () processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device). eval () Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech: conversation = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "Respond with interleaved text and audio." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : [{ "type" : "audio" , "audio" : "question.wav" }]}, { "role" : "assistant" , "content" : "<|mixed_start|>" }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, continue_final_message= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(device) with torch.no_grad(): outputs = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 1024 , audio_temperature= 1.0 , audio_top_k= 128 , audio_repetition_penalty= 1.1 , audio_repetition_window= 4096 , return_dict_in_generate= True , ) text = processor.decode( outputs.sequences[ 0 , inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:], skip_special_tokens= True , ) waveform = codec.decode( outputs.audio_codes[: 1 , :, :outputs.audio_lengths[ 0 ]] ).audio_values[ 0 ] # 24 kHz print (text) sf.write( "reply.wav" , waveform. float ().cpu().numpy(), 24_000 ) See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling. LFM3-Omni-2B Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card . To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch torchvision torchcodec accelerate pillow librosa soundfile import torch import soundfile as sf from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Omni-2B" device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32 model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code= True ). eval () processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device). eval () Then ask a question about a photo by voice: conversation = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "Answer questions about the provided image. Base every answer only on what can be seen. Respond with text." , }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : "photo.jpg" }, { "type" : "audio" , "audio" : "question.wav" }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(device) with torch.no_grad(): outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 1024 , generation_mode= "text" ) print (processor.decode( outputs.sequences[ 0 , inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:outputs.sequence_lengths[ 0 ]], skip_special_tokens= True , )) See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling. d1-2B and d1-omni-2B Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. items.content: Back to Articles Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software Enterprise Article Published October 29, 2026 Upvote 33 +27 Kate Soule katesoule Follow ibm-granite Luis A Lastras GrizleeBer Follow ibm-granite Subhajit Chaudhury subhajit1412 Follow ibm-granite Abraham Daniels abedaniels Follow ibm-granite Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1 , showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint. Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood. Updated Granite Speech ASR model — multilingual speech-to-text across 10 languages with native punctuation and capitalization, so transcripts are ready for downstream models without a formatting pass. Updated Decision adapter in granitelib-core — featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set. While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy. This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. items.content: Back to Articles StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents Enterprise Article Published November 3, 2026 Upvote 7 +1 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 📄 Tech Report | 🤗 Data | 💻 Code We’re introducing StateBench , a benchmark for long-context state tracking —how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve. State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack. Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds. To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer. Four levels of state tracking StateBench consists of four difficulty levels that permit increasingly complex state update operations. For programmers, these levels of state tracking complexity can be understood as allowing different types of variable assignment operations: R-trivial problems use immutable assignment. A variable’s value never changes, so the model only needs to recover what it was first set to. In code, this looks like let x = 4; in everyday life, it’s like a birth date—it stays fixed. Aperiodic problems allow reassignment by value. The model needs to find the most recent value and can ignore earlier ones. In code, this looks like x = 4 followed later by x = 2; in everyday life, it’s like a thermostat, where the latest setting determines the current temperature. Soluble problems add self-referential updates. Each update builds on the current value, so the model has to carry changes forward rather than simply find the latest assignment. In code, this looks like x = x + 5; in everyday life, it’s like a game score, where each point adds to the running total. General finite problems add assignment by reference. One variable can take on another variable’s current value, creating dependencies across updates. In code, this looks like x = y or swapping two variables. Imagine a magician hiding a ball under one of five cups, then repeatedly swapping their positions. Finding the ball means keeping track of how those swaps change its location. This illustrates the S₅ state-tracking problem: following how successive swaps rearrange five objects. It belongs to the hardest of our four levels and is discussed in previous work on the limits of state tracking . These levels can be intuitively understood in terms of variable assignments, but they also represent theoretically motivated distinctions in state tracking rooted in Krohn–Rhodes theory, a branch of algebra that describes how state-tracking problems – which can be viewed as word problems over finite monoids – can be decomposed into atomic primitives. Each level in our hierarchy corresponds to a class of state-tracking problems that can be built out of a different set of primitives. To compare the four levels fairly, we start with a general finite sequence of variable assignments and derive three easier versions from it, producing four comparable StateBench problems—one at each difficulty level. All four use the same number of variables and distinct values, with assignments appearing at the same points in the sequence; only the type of assignment changes. What we found Pretrained models We tested a range of open pretrained models on the r-trivial, aperiodic, and general finite levels of StateBench to see where their state tracking breaks down, and whether different architectures fail where theory predicts. Under standard theoretical assumptions, transformers can handle r-trivial robustly (and soluble and aperiodic to some degree) but are predicted to fail on general problems. In contrast, Gated DeltaNet with a more flexible memory update can, in principle, handle all four levels. We started with open pretrained models, where the training data and context lengths are fully documented. These included two 7-billion-parameter models, Olmo 3 (a transformer) and Olmo Hybrid (which adds Gated DeltaNet layers), along with smaller models with 275 million and 2.7 billion parameters. All of these models were pretrained on the same data; none had seen contexts longer than 64,000 tokens during training, and we tested most of them on inputs well beyond that length. When we scored each model, almost all performed well on r-trivial problems, lost accuracy on aperiodic ones as inputs grew, and stayed at chance on general finite problems. Problem format mattered here—the 275-million-parameter hybrid and Gated DeltaNet models scored near the ceiling on RULER-style r-trivial problems but were near chance on the same problems framed as spreadsheet edits. That gap is one reason StateBench tests the same underlying problem in several formats. Frontier models We then tested four frontier models – Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna – asking them to read each sequence of variable assignments and generate the final value of every variable. All four performed well on r-trivial and aperiodic problems. But on soluble and general finite problems, accuracy fell sharply as inputs grew longer, dropping to 13% or lower on the longest general finite problems. One likely factor is sensitivity ; at these harder levels, many more steps can affect the final answer, leaving less room for a model to miss an update without getting the result wrong. Models trained directly on the task Next, we investigated whether models’ difficulty with the harder levels reflects limits of the architectures themselves, or whether pretraining simply doesn’t teach models to solve them. Targeted direct training is a more favorable setting that reveals to what degree state-tracking issues come from the underlying architecture and optimizer rather than the data used to pretrain a model. We trained several 275-million-parameter models from scratch on StateBench: two transformer variants, two hybrids, and two Gated DeltaNet variants with different memory-update constraints. The models trained on sequences of up to 256 assignments and were tested on sequences as long as 64,000 assignments, or 250 times the maximum training length. The architectures began to diverge as sequences grew longer. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on r-trivial, aperiodic, and soluble problems out to the longest sequences we tested, tens of thousands of assignments. Transformers learned the easier levels but degraded on longer sequences, and they never learned general finite problems. On the hardest level, the Gated DeltaNet variant with a more flexible memory update generalized the farthest, staying near perfect out to roughly 10 times the length of the longest sequences it saw during training. For Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models, the gap points to training rather than architecture; trained directly, they learned to handle state-tracking levels their pretrained counterparts couldn’t. Transformers were different—even trained directly, they could never learn the hardest level. Open questions and the release Some questions remain open. Our new proof shows that Gated DeltaNet with a more limited memory update (non-negative eigenvalues) can solve all aperiodic tasks and certain periodic tasks, such as tracking whether a repeated input has occurred an even or odd number of times, under the paper’s fixed-precision arithmetic with rounding. Its exact placement in the hierarchy remains open, including whether it can solve all soluble tasks and how numerical precision or combining it with attention layers affects its capabilities. StateBench also assumes a fixed number of variables, while real tasks often introduce new entities over time. In a long conversation, for example, new people and objects can appear as it unfolds, and the model has to begin tracking them too. The current framework doesn’t yet cover that setting. As new flavors of recurrent and hybrid architectures emerge, understanding which kinds of state tracking each can handle could help guide how future systems are developed and trained. We hope StateBench gives researchers a finer-grained way to find where models break down—and to build training and evaluation data for the capabilities that still fall short. More fundamentally, we hope it serves as a North Star for researchers to develop new architectures with more robust state-tracking abilities compared to current models. items.content: Back to Articles Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language Enterprise Article Published November 3, 2026 Upvote 5 Praveen Venkateswaran praveenv Follow ibm-research Anupama Murthi anupamamurthi Follow ibm-research Hamid Adebayo harmedox Follow ibm-research Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all. Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other. Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language , and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it. Why decks are hard for small models A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at. It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from. It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent. There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them. Build it like a human: a designer and a coder Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter: The designer reads the plan and writes a structured JSON brief: the palette, the type system, and for each slide its layout, its exact content and a short design rationale. The coder takes one slide's spec from the brief and writes the pptxgenjs JavaScript that draws it, preceded by its reasoning. Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster. We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×. Synthesizing decks and their reasoning There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides. Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example: "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance." The coder reasons about geometry: "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart." The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example. The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest. What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions. Steering a deck in plain English Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives , short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]] : ## Rollout plan - March: pilot with two teams - May: security review complete - July: rollout to all of engineering - September: company-wide launch - November: first adoption review [[make this a timeline]] The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead. The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase. Category Example directive Layout [[make this a timeline]] Tone [[be candid, no spin]] Audience [[this is for the board]] Order [[lead with the ask]] Leaving out [[no pricing]] Emphasis [[highlight the headline number]] Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive. Building a check-and-repair harness Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first. Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned. First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code. The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse. Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right). To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average. Evaluation We evaluate on PresentBench , which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper. Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean. Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model. PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close. What's next The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all. Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other. Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language , and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. Why decks are hard for small models A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at. It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from. It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent. There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them. Build it like a human: a designer and a coder Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter: The designer reads the plan and writes a structured JSON brief: the palette, the type system, and for each slide its layout, its exact content and a short design rationale. The coder takes one slide's spec from the brief and writes the pptxgenjs JavaScript that draws it, preceded by its reasoning. Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster. We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×. Synthesizing decks and their reasoning There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides. Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example: "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance." The coder reasons about geometry: "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart." The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example. The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest. What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions. Steering a deck in plain English Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives , short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]] : ## Rollout plan - March: pilot with two teams - May: security review complete - July: rollout to all of engineering - September: company-wide launch - November: first adoption review [[make this a timeline]] The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead. The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase. Category Example directive Layout [[make this a timeline]] Tone [[be candid, no spin]] Audience [[this is for the board]] Order [[lead with the ask]] Leaving out [[no pricing]] Emphasis [[highlight the headline number]] Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive. Building a check-and-repair harness Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first. Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned. First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code. The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse. Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. items.content: Back to Articles Transformers Model Integration Contracts Published November 3, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 12 +6 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months. When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it. Why bugs reach main Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels. The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main. Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study , the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB. This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU. Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine. Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main. Introducing Model Integration Contracts transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts: a fixture : the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned a usage path : a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the model, such as generating text or running a training step baselines : the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a human The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines. A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic . For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt: inputs = tokenizer( "The capital of France is" , return_tensors= "pt" ) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 4 , do_sample= False ) new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:] print (tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens= True )) It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md . A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later. On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes. The UMT5 regression We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28 . Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20. One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint. We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup. The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details. How models are shrunk The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear. The recipe now has four steps: Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds, including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers. Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible. We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name. Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte. Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test. Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds. Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR. We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail. The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style. Building MICs with agents Our CLI, tmic , creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review. To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model : pip install "transformers-mic[runtime]" "hf-doc-builder @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/doc-builder.git" hf auth login tmic run org/model --local-only --fixtures-only --no-history --bill-to '' It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account ( --bill-to '' ). The CLI docs cover the individual steps. We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space . Random vs Overfit With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path. So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study , the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24. That gives us two ways to build the weights: Start with random weights and a fixed seed. Overfit on a few examples, like "The capital of France is" => "Paris". The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed. So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both. Open questions As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet: How many real bugs does it catch on PRs, not just in replays? How often does it send us chasing false alarms? How much work do baseline reviews take? We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss. Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for. Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs. Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space , try the tmic workflow , and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract. Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs. Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space , try the tmic workflow , and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.03633 (cs) [Submitted on 2 Nov 2026] Title: Pretraining Data Scale Reverses the Muon-AdamW Fine-Tuning Gap Authors: Catherine Li , Jingchu Gai , Andrej Risteski , Jacob Mitchell Springer , Aditi Raghunathan View a PDF of the paper titled Pretraining Data Scale Reverses the Muon-AdamW Fine-Tuning Gap, by Catherine Li and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Muon has recently emerged as a promising optimizer for pretraining large language models, offering a speedup over AdamW in minimizing pretraining loss. However, it remains unclear whether Muon's advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token-parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training. items.content: Pretraining Data Scale Reverses the Muon–AdamW Fine-Tuning Gap Abstract Muon has recently emerged as a promising optimizer for pretraining large language models, offering a speedup over AdamW in minimizing pretraining loss. However, it remains unclear whether Muon’s advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token–parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training. Catherine Li ∗ Jingchu Gai ∗ Andrej Risteski Jacob Mitchell Springer † Aditi Raghunathan † Carnegie Mellon University {catheri4, jgai}@andrew.cmu.edu 1 Introduction The Muon optimizer has recently shown strong empirical performance for pretraining LLMs, challenging AdamW’s status as the standard optimizer for minimizing pretraining loss ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) . Prior work has shown that the pretraining optimization choices that minimize pretraining loss do not necessarily yield the best model after fine-tuning ( Watts et al., 2026 ) . What ultimately matters downstream is the learning–forgetting tradeoff : how well a fine-tuned model learns the target task while retaining its pretrained knowledge. Motivated by this, we ask: Does Muon’s pretraining advantage over AdamW extend to the learning–forgetting tradeoff? To answer this question, we measure the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap , which compares the two optimizers on this tradeoff; a negative gap indicates that the Muon pretrained model dominates the AdamW pretrained model after fine-tuning, and a positive gap indicates the reverse. We show that the answer depends on the pretraining data budget, and find that pretraining data scale reverses the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap . At small budgets, Muon achieves lower fine-tuning loss with less forgetting than AdamW and the fine-tuning gap is negative. At larger budgets, this trend reverses: AdamW achieves a better learning–forgetting tradeoff than Muon, and the fine-tuning gap becomes positive. In Section 3 , we pretrain OLMo-style 30M–600M models ( Groeneveld et al., 2024 ; Team OLMo et al., 2025 ) on 150 150 M to 154 154 B DCLM tokens ( Li et al., 2024 ) , comparing AdamW and Muon, and fine-tune each base model on four datasets while sweeping the fine-tuning optimizer and learning rate, for nearly 600 pretraining runs and 29,000 fine-tuning runs in total. We show that when tuning pretraining hyperparameters for the lowest pretraining loss, Muon consistently achieves lower loss than AdamW. However, with sufficient pretraining data, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning, reversing the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap. This reversal also holds when we disregard pretraining loss, instead sweeping pretraining hyperparameters to obtain the best learning–forgetting tradeoff after fine-tuning. We additionally show that as model size scales, AdamW surpasses Muon at progressively smaller data budgets . In Section 4 , we investigate why the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap reverses as the pretraining data budget grows. Fine-tuning changes the output distribution, so we generalize fine-tuning updates with perturbations to the output distribution and study which optimizer produces base models that are more robust to such perturbations. To quantify sensitivity to output perturbations, we introduce the margin-to-spread ratio (MSR) , a simple metric derived from the model’s output logits that characterizes robustness. For each prediction, the MSR is the difference between the correct logit and the average of the incorrect logits, normalized by the spread of the incorrect logits ( Section 4.1 ): a prediction is more robust when the MSR is larger. Figure 1: Beyond a sufficiently large data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon. We pretrain OLMo-60M models with Muon and AdamW and fine-tune on StackMathQA. For each pretraining optimizer, we take the pretrained model with the lowest pretraining loss, sweep across all fine-tuning configurations, and plot the resulting learning–forgetting frontier, from 2.4 2.4 B to 38.4 38.4 B pretraining tokens. At 2.4 2.4 B tokens, Muon’s frontier dominates AdamW’s; at larger budgets the trend reverses and AdamW surpasses Muon. This reversal happens despite Muon achieving lower pretraining loss across all data budgets. To understand where this trend comes from, we study a linear associative memory trained with gradient descent (GD) and Muon ( Section 4.2 ). Analyzing a single update from zero initialization, we prove that the ratio of GD’s MSR to Muon’s increases with the data budget ( Section 4.2 ). Simulations of many training steps in the linear associative memory setting confirm the same trend: Muon has the larger MSR at small data budgets, while GD has the larger MSR at large data budgets ( Section 4.2 ). Measuring the MSR of our pretrained language models, we find that Muon has the larger MSR at small data budgets, while AdamW has the larger MSR at large data budgets, mirroring the reversal of the fine-tuning gap ( Section 4.3 ). 2 Preliminaries Our goal is to compare AdamW- and Muon-pretrained models after fine-tuning . Since fine-tuning can induce forgetting of the pretraining distribution, performance on the fine-tuning task alone is not sufficient: one base model may learn more but also forget more. We therefore compare base models by the tradeoff between the two, and define metrics to track how this comparison changes with model size and pretraining data budget. Let θ PT \theta_{\mathrm{PT}} denote a pretrained model. Learning–forgetting tradeoff. Fine-tuning improves downstream performance but may degrade pretrained knowledge ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 ; Springer et al., 2025 ) . When θ PT \theta_{\mathrm{PT}} is fine-tuned to obtain θ FT \theta_{\mathrm{FT}} , we measure learning by the fine-tuning loss ℒ FT ​ ( θ FT ) \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{FT}}) and forgetting by the pretraining loss ℒ PT ​ ( θ FT ) \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{FT}}) . Since both depend on the fine-tuning hyperparameters, a single fine-tuned checkpoint does not capture how well θ PT \theta_{\mathrm{PT}} can be adapted. We therefore summarize each base model by the outcomes reachable by fine-tuning it, 𝒯 ⁡ ( θ PT ) ≔ { ( ℒ FT ​ ( θ FT ) , ℒ PT ​ ( θ FT ) ) | θ FT ∈ Θ FT ​ ( θ PT ) } , \mathcal{T}(\theta_{\mathrm{PT}})\coloneqq\left\{\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{FT}}),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{FT}})\bigr)\,\middle|\,\theta_{\mathrm{FT}}\in\Theta_{\mathrm{FT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{PT}})\right\}, where Θ FT ​ ( θ PT ) \Theta_{\mathrm{FT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{PT}}) is the set of models obtained by fine-tuning θ PT \theta_{\mathrm{PT}} , and compare base models through the lower-left Pareto frontier of this set, which we call the learning–forgetting frontier . For a collection of base models ℬ \mathcal{B} , we compare the corresponding sets 𝒯 ⁡ ( ℬ ) ≔ { 𝒯 ⁡ ( θ PT ) ∣ θ PT ∈ ℬ } . \mathcal{T}(\mathcal{B})\coloneqq\{\mathcal{T}(\theta_{\mathrm{PT}})\mid\theta_{\mathrm{PT}}\in\mathcal{B}\}. Fine-tuning gap. We compare the two optimizers on this tradeoff with a single metric, fine-tuning gap G FT G_{\mathrm{FT}} , which we define as the signed mean minimum Euclidean distance between the AdamW and Muon frontier. The fine-tuning gap is positive when the AdamW frontier dominates the Muon frontier, and the reverse else wise. items.raw_text: Pretraining Data Scale Reverses the Muon–AdamW Fine-Tuning Gap Abstract Muon has recently emerged as a promising optimizer for pretraining large language models, offering a speedup over AdamW in minimizing pretraining loss. However, it remains unclear whether Muon’s advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token–parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training. Prior work has shown that the pretraining optimization choices that minimize pretraining loss do not necessarily yield the best model after fine-tuning ( Watts et al., 2026 ) . What ultimately matters downstream is the learning–forgetting tradeoff : how well a fine-tuned model learns the target task while retaining its pretrained knowledge. Motivated by this, we ask: Does Muon’s pretraining advantage over AdamW extend to the learning–forgetting tradeoff? To answer this question, we measure the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap , which compares the two optimizers on this tradeoff; a negative gap indicates that the Muon pretrained model dominates the AdamW pretrained model after fine-tuning, and a positive gap indicates the reverse. We show that the answer depends on the pretraining data budget, and find that pretraining data scale reverses the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap . At small budgets, Muon achieves lower fine-tuning loss with less forgetting than AdamW and the fine-tuning gap is negative. At larger budgets, this trend reverses: AdamW achieves a better learning–forgetting tradeoff than Muon, and the fine-tuning gap becomes positive. In Section 3 , we pretrain OLMo-style 30M–600M models ( Groeneveld et al., 2024 ; Team OLMo et al., 2025 ) on 150 150 M to 154 154 B DCLM tokens ( Li et al., 2024 ) , comparing AdamW and Muon, and fine-tune each base model on four datasets while sweeping the fine-tuning optimizer and learning rate, for nearly 600 pretraining runs and 29,000 fine-tuning runs in total. This reversal also holds when we disregard pretraining loss, instead sweeping pretraining hyperparameters to obtain the best learning–forgetting tradeoff after fine-tuning. We additionally show that as model size scales, AdamW surpasses Muon at progressively smaller data budgets . items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.03627 (cs) [Submitted on 2 Nov 2026] Title: Not All Reasoning Generalizes: A Case Study on Learning Generalizable Reasoning Strategies in RLVR Authors: Ziqi Pang , Yu-Xiong Wang View a PDF of the paper titled Not All Reasoning Generalizes: A Case Study on Learning Generalizable Reasoning Strategies in RLVR, by Ziqi Pang and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can enable generalizable improvement for large language model (LLM) reasoning. This paper studies how to incentivize such generalization via reasoning strategies. We study this question with a controllable equation-solving framework: finding multiple inputs x for equations f(x)=y, where f is a non-bijective string function. This setting makes reasoning strategies observable while supporting a clear definition of easy-to-hard out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts, e.g., more solutions, longer y, etc. We uncover a subtle RLVR failure: it teaches the model to solve in-distribution tasks with high accuracy and structured step-by-step derivation, yet under OOD shifts, the same model abandons derivation and collapses to ineffective brute-force enumeration, causing sharp accuracy drops. This observation reveals the deeper challenges of RLVR generalization as it is neither incapable base model nor reward hacking, since the model succeeds in-distribution with the correct reasoning strategy. The key to mitigating this failure is an indirect intervention that surprisingly helps: co-training with bijective inversion tasks. Although these bijective tasks are actually not uniformly harder and even further from the non-bijective OOD evaluation, they make derivation more certain and substantially restore the correct strategy and accuracy under OOD shifts. This effect further motivates our theoretical analysis: outcome-only RLVR can shape reasoning processes through implicitly crediting the effective reasoning strategies more, even without process supervision. To conclude, our analysis framework and findings systematically reveal the crucial role and incentivization of reasoning strategies in RLVR generalization under OOD shifts. items.content: Not All Reasoning Generalizes: A Case Study on Learning Generalizable Reasoning Strategies in RLVR Ziqi Pang Yu-Xiong Wang Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Email: {ziqip2,yxw}@illinois.edu Abstract Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can enable generalizable improvement for large language model (LLM) reasoning. This paper studies how to incentivize such generalization via reasoning strategies . We study this question with a controllable equation-solving framework: finding multiple inputs x x for equations f ⁡ ( x ) = y f(x)=y , where f f is a non-bijective string function. This setting makes reasoning strategies observable while supporting a clear definition of easy-to-hard out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts, e.g. , more solutions, longer y y , etc. We uncover a subtle RLVR failure: it teaches the model to solve in-distribution tasks with high accuracy and structured step-by-step derivation, yet under OOD shifts, the same model abandons derivation and collapses to ineffective brute-force enumeration, causing sharp accuracy drops. This observation reveals the deeper challenges of RLVR generalization as it is neither incapable base model nor reward hacking , since the model succeeds in-distribution with the correct reasoning strategy. The key to mitigating this failure is an indirect intervention that surprisingly helps: co-training with bijective inversion tasks. Although these bijective tasks are actually not uniformly harder and even further from the non-bijective OOD evaluation, they make derivation more certain and substantially restore the correct strategy and accuracy under OOD shifts. This effect further motivates our theoretical analysis: outcome-only RLVR can shape reasoning processes through implicitly crediting the effective reasoning strategies more, even without process supervision. To conclude, our analysis framework and findings systematically reveal the crucial role and incentivization of reasoning strategies in RLVR generalization under OOD shifts. Code is available at https://github.com/ziqipang/rl_meta_thinking . 1 Introduction Applying reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) to large language models (LLMs) has shown surprising generalization capabilities. Rather than imitating fixed traces, RLVR incentivizes meta-level reasoning strategies that can transfer to out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks. For instance, Yuan et al. (2026) ; Liu et al. (2026a) show that general reasoning strategies like composing and case analysis are shown to be transferable from the training tasks to novel domains ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . Such positive cases, however, cannot establish transfer as a general rule. We ask the complementary question: when and why does RLVR generalization fail? However, we realize that such generalization of reasoning strategies has not been thoroughly investigated. Previous studies mostly understand RLVR generalization from its relationship with the base models ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) without clearly categorizing individual reasoning strategies and analyzing their OOD generalization. To this end, we start by building a controllable framework that clearly defines OOD generalization and categorizes reasoning strategies. As in Fig. 1 a , we construct a set of string functions f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) inspired by Yuan et al. (2026) , and let the LLM address this inverse problem: recovering multiple inputs x x such that f ⁡ ( x ) = y f(x)=y ( y y is a provided string output). This task mirrors solving math equations and tracing bugs in coding. More importantly, we construct the functions f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) f(\cdot) to be non-bijective and require LLMs to output k > 1 k>1 different solutions. This framework thus clearly splits in-distribution and OOD tasks, where the OOD tasks are built from held-out functions and made harder via longer strings y y and more required solutions k k . On this controllable framework, we observe that RLVR can reliably teach an LLM to perform reasoning effectively in-distribution , showing reliable derivation strategies step-by-step and enumerating characters only when needed, as Fig. 1 b . However, this model, named Mono , shows drastically different behaviors on harder OOD tasks: it abandons the strategy of derivation, and instead, relies on ineffective brute-force enumeration of all the digits simultaneously (Fig. 1 c ). Such an observation marks an important revelation: an LLM can learn to perform effective reasoning strategies in-distribution , yet drastically falls back to worse strategies in OOD scenarios . Such an observation is nuanced as it is not related to the commonly known RLVR failures like incapable base models or reward hacking, as the model is following valid reasoning traces to achieve high accuracy during training. Therefore, we are studying real generalization challenges under this setting. Figure 1: (a) To clearly define OOD generalization for LLM reasoning, we construct a controllable framework via solving string function equations, mirroring real-world math and coding. (b) We categorize two major reasoning strategies, the more effective Derivation and or total brute-force Enumeration . (c) We reveal how reasoning strategies reflect the challenges of OOD generalization. The Mono model learns derivation for ID cases, yet drastically collapses to enumeration for OOD. With Mixed better incentivizing the derivation strategy, it achieves much better OOD accuracy under similar ID performance. These form a systematic framework of understanding RLVR generalization. This diagnosis suggests that the key is not merely to improve training accuracy but to change which reasoning strategies RLVR incentivizes. We therefore introduce a seemingly indirect intervention for the task: co-training with bijective tasks that only asks for one solution x x for f ⁡ ( x ) = y f(x)=y . The intuition is to decrease the search space in non-bijective functions and encourage step-by-step derivation with larger certainties. Importantly, this intervention is surprising because the bijective tasks are not uniformly harder and are even further away from the non-bijective OOD evaluation requiring multiple solutions. Nevertheless, the Mixed model with this intervention successfully restores the behavior of utilizing the derivation strategy and leads to significantly better OOD accuracy (Fig. 1 c ). Such effectiveness inspires us to understand how better reasoning strategies can be incentivized from RLVR. As in Fig. 1 b , we view the reasoning process as progressively shrinking the candidate solution space. This analogy clearly distinguishes the derivation and enumeration: derivation is more effective by structurally pruning multiple candidates in a single step, while enumeration can only contribute marginally by eliminating one wrong candidate. Therefore, the reasoning strategies like derivation can contribute more bits per step, and can more easily generalize to harder scenarios, i.e. , those requiring more bits. By connecting this with RL algorithms theoretically, we show that even outcome-only RLVR can implicitly credit such effective reasoning processes without process supervision, explaining how reasoning strategies could emerge from RLVR. Beyond theory, our probing of the hidden states and reasoning trace audit also qualitatively shows how reasoning strategies could be a principled way to understand the generalization behaviors of LLMs in RLVR. Our study presents a systematic analysis of RLVR generalization via reasoning strategies: (i) A controlled counter-example of RLVR teaching correct in-distribution reasoning strategies that nevertheless change and fail under OOD shifts : a subtle failure distinct from incapable base models. (ii) A principled intervention on reasoning strategies significantly enhances OOD generalization, which reveals the pivotal role of reasoning strategies in the transferable improvements of RLVR. (iii) The theoretical analysis explaining how more effective and generalizable reasoning strategies can be incentivized naturally via RLVR from a information per reasoning step perspective. (iv) Reasoning trace inspection and probing of the model’s hidden states qualitatively reveal how reasoning strategies are principled aspects to understand RLVR generalization. Considering the importance of RLVR generalization, we hope this framework has provided a comprehensive yet nuanced understanding of LLM reasoning and generalization through synthetic and controllable data, with the same spirit as prior work that has inspired us ( Allen-Zhu & Li, 2025a ; Ye et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Yin et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . 2 Related Work RLVR Generalization. RLVR has produced a growing set of positive generalization results: such as general reasoning and agentic capabilities enhancement after math/coding-oriented RL ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Kimi Team et al., 2025 ) , carefully structured RL expands benchmark coverage ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) , synthetic strings showing compositional expansion ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) , and game/puzzles improve to reasoning benchmarks ( Liu et al., 2026a ; Zhao et al., 2025a ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Tong et al., 2026 ) . Synthetic data is a crucial tool to analyze the LLM behaviors reliably, especially represented by the physics of LLMs ( Allen-Zhu & Li, 2025a ; Ye et al., 2025a ; Ye et al., 2025b ; Allen-Zhu & Li, 2024 ; Allen-Zhu & Li, 2025b ; Allen-Zhu & Li, 2025c ) .
