Our investigation centers on which reasoning strategy RLVR incentivizes, and whether the learned strategy generalizes from in-distribution training to OOD scenarios or quietly collapses. We therefore propose a research framework that surfaces the model’s reasoning process and admits a controlled distribution shift between training and evaluation. The principles are: (1) Clean OOD Generalization. We adopt synthetic tasks following prior controlled LLM studies ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Chu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2025a ) , enabling a clean separation between the training and testing distributions for studying OOD generalization. (2) Explicit Reasoning Strategies. To diagnose reasoning strategies, the tasks must surface a small set of clearly identifiable strategies. The open-ended flexibility of real-world math or coding tasks works against this need for clean strategy categorization. (3) Reasoning Strategy Diversity. While the strategies must be categorizable, the framework must also allow multiple candidate strategies, so that generalization can be studied by observing which one RLVR selects. From this aspect, the homogeneous function-simulation tasks in Yuan et al. (2026) fall short, as they only exercise the “composing” reasoning strategy and calculation of function outputs. The Inversion Task. We instantiate these principles via an inversion task on synthetic string functions, which reverses the direction of Yuan et al. (2026) : given the source code of a function f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) f(\cdot) and a target output y y , the LLM is asked to recover one or more digit-string inputs x x satisfying f ⁡ ( x ) = y f(x)=y . This mirrors two real-world reasoning settings: solving math equations, where one reasons backward from a constraint to its solutions, and tracing program bugs, where one infers an upstream cause from an observed output. Crucially, the inversion task admits several reward-compatible strategies: analytical derivation, case analysis, and brute-force enumeration. It thus satisfies principles (2) and (3), while the next subsection addresses principle (1). 3.2 Task Design We turn the inversion task above into a concrete training-and-evaluation suite, including (i) a library of functions with a function-level train/held-out split, (ii) OOD tests that probe the learned strategy for easy-to-hard generalization, and (iii) evaluation metrics. Function Design for Held-out Training/Evaluation. We construct the training and testing sets to use distinct functions f f , preventing the LLM from memorizing function-specific patterns. We therefore compose 24 non-bijective functions (many-to-one, so one output y y has multiple valid inputs x x ) (full list in Sec. A.2 ) and provide their definitions and Python code inside the prompt of every inversion task. Following Yuan et al. (2026) , we split these functions into training and evaluation sets: 18 functions are used for RL training, and 6 strictly disjoint functions are held out for evaluation. This held-out slice forms the easiest test of generalization: same prompt interface, same input/output regime, only the underlying function is unseen. It serves as the in-distribution check that RLVR has learned to perform inversion. From this baseline, we then move to the easy-to-hard OOD generalization tests below, which are our main probe of reasoning-strategy generalization. The training set contains 50k tasks, and each evaluation set contains 1,024 tasks. Easy-to-hard OOD Generalization. As Fig. 1 a , we design the in-domain and OOD tasks to differ along controlled axes. For the inversion task f ⁡ ( x ) = y f(x)=y , the in-domain scenarios train and evaluate the LLM on outputs y y of length 4–6 and require 2 candidate solutions per prompt. From this baseline, we design four easy-to-hard OOD axes: (1) More Answers raises the number of requested solutions to a random integer between 3 and 6, demanding more computation and reliability to produce enough valid solutions. (2) Longer Outputs increases the target output to length 6–10, lengthening the digit chain that must be inverted. (3) Longer Outputs & More Answers combines the two axes above. (4) Length Change represents the largest shift: our in-distribution function family is designed so that y y and x x share the same length, but the Length-Change functions differ in the lengths of y y and x x (full list in Sec. A.2 ). Each OOD evaluation set contains 1,024 randomly generated tasks as above. Accuracy Scoring. We compute accuracy based on whether the predicted solutions are correct with an outcome-based verifier. Each solution is scored semantically by executing the reference function and checking whether its output matches y y . Let k k be the effective answer requirement and m m be the number of submitted solutions; accuracy is acc = min ⁡ ( correct_unique , k ) / max ⁡ ( k , m ) \mathrm{acc}=\min(\text{correct\_unique},k)/\max(k,m) . This rewards answers that are both distinct and correct, and penalizes over-generation reward hacking. 3.3 Training We train Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) and adopt the improvements from DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , especially the filtering of groups with zero reward variance. This filtering is crucial both in the early stage of training, when the LLM is still developing its strategy with low accuracy, and in the late stage, when in-distribution accuracy has been high. We select this base model because our synthetic task lies on the boundary of its capabilities, requiring RL to incentivize correct reasoning strategies. Design details are in Sec. A.3 . Analysis of more base models in Sec. A.4 . 4 Reasoning Strategy Collapse and Generalization This section reveals the collapse and generalization of reasoning strategies in OOD tasks. We first show how the reasoning strategies collapse in OOD tasks despite crrect in-distribution behaviors (Sec. 4.1 ). Then, we introduce incentivizing a better reasoning strategy for generalization (Sec. 4.2 ). The Mono model performs normally ID but collapses, which relies on brute-force enumeration OOD. In comparison, Mixed model shows similar ID performance, but surprisingly doubles analytical derivation reasoning on OOD and lead to better generalization. These reveal the challenges of reasoning strategy generalization and how to enhance the generalization of reasoning in RLVR. 4.1 Mono Model: Revealing OOD Collapse of Reasoning Strategies Following Sec. 3 , we train the LLM on the non-bijective function inversion tasks, i.e. , solving x x given f ⁡ ( x ) = y f(x)=y , and call this model Mono . By closely observing it on the in-distribution and the four easy-to-hard OOD sets, as in Fig. 2 , we observe the nuanced OOD reasoning strategy collapse. Reasoning Strategy Categorization. Our synthetic tasks are specially constructed to understand the RLVR reasoning strategy generalization in a controllable way, as explained in Sec. 3.1 . So we Figure 3: Examples of reasoning strategies. start from categorizing the reasoning strategy utilized by the Mono model. As in Fig. 3 , we can clearly attribute two primary strategies: derivation , which structurally reverses f f and only conduct case-analysis when needed, and enumeration , which directly guess all the digits all at once, being much less efficient. To make this binary classification revealing the traits of reasoning strategies, we treat purely brute-force enumeration as “enumeration,” and everything else as “derivation.” In practice, we employ an LLM judge empowered by Gemini-3.0-Flash to classify the reasoning traces (clarification of our setup, details, and verification of LLM judge in Sec. B.1 ). From ID to OOD Collapse. Fig. 2(a) tracks accuracy during RL on the ID set and the four OOD sets, and Fig. 2(b) shows which strategies produce these responses. On in-distribution tasks, the Mono model learns the effective strategy of derivation in most cases and achieves high accuracy (as Fig. 2 , ID columns). Rather, its reasoning skill of derivation acquired disappears on OOD tasks and gives way to the inefficient brute-force enumeration, which proposes all the digits of x x simultaneously, without utilizing the structure of the function f f . The majority of failures are caused by loops that enumerate all possible digits until reaching the token limits. Takeaway 1 Reasoning Strategy Collapse: Even though RLVR has incentivized the correct reasoning strategies for in-distribution tasks, the LLM might drastically change to ineffective strategies on OOD tasks despite identical task formats, undermining the generalization of RLVR. 4.2 Mixed Model: Enhancing OOD Generalization via Bijective Inversion The derivation reasoning strategy, avoiding pure enumeration, is thus our key to understanding RLVR generalization. Our intervention, therefore, is not to propose training tasks that are closer to the evaluation or simply harder than the existing training tasks, but a set of new tasks that more directly incentivize the derivation strategy. In fact, this is also why RLVR could bring improvements to multiple reasoning domains for LLMs in previous works ( Liu et al., 2026a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . Specifically, we propose using bijective functions as f f (both injective and surjective) to eliminate uncertainty in non-bijective tasks and encourage derivation via larger certainty. Enhancing OOD Generalization. Concretely, we co-train on bijective inversion with a 1 : 1 1{:}1 with the original non-bijective tasks, so this model is called Mixed . As shown in Fig. 2(b) , this almost doubles the utilization of derivation strategy compared with the Mono model, and leads to significantly better OOD evaluation (Fig. 2(a) ), especially on the novel functions of LenChange. Therefore, the incorporation of bijective inversion effectively improves the RLVR reasoning generalization. We have controlled the data recipe and training configuration for a fair comparison between the two models (details Sec. A.3 ) and additionally verified the main conclusions with multiple runs in Sec. B.2.4 .

This paper studies how to incentivize such generalization via reasoning strategies . We study this question with a controllable equation-solving framework: finding multiple inputs x x for equations f ⁡ ( x ) = y f(x)=y , where f f is a non-bijective string function. This setting makes reasoning strategies observable while supporting a clear definition of easy-to-hard out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts, e.g. , more solutions, longer y y , etc. We uncover a subtle RLVR failure: it teaches the model to solve in-distribution tasks with high accuracy and structured step-by-step derivation, yet under OOD shifts, the same model abandons derivation and collapses to ineffective brute-force enumeration, causing sharp accuracy drops. This observation reveals the deeper challenges of RLVR generalization as it is neither incapable base model nor reward hacking , since the model succeeds in-distribution with the correct reasoning strategy. The key to mitigating this failure is an indirect intervention that surprisingly helps: co-training with bijective inversion tasks. Although these bijective tasks are actually not uniformly harder and even further from the non-bijective OOD evaluation, they make derivation more certain and substantially restore the correct strategy and accuracy under OOD shifts. This effect further motivates our theoretical analysis: outcome-only RLVR can shape reasoning processes through implicitly crediting the effective reasoning strategies more, even without process supervision. To conclude, our analysis framework and findings systematically reveal the crucial role and incentivization of reasoning strategies in RLVR generalization under OOD shifts. Code is available at https://github.com/ziqipang/rl_meta_thinking . 1 Introduction Applying reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) to large language models (LLMs) has shown surprising generalization capabilities. Rather than imitating fixed traces, RLVR incentivizes meta-level reasoning strategies that can transfer to out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks. For instance, Yuan et al. (2026) ; Liu et al. (2026a) show that general reasoning strategies like composing and case analysis are shown to be transferable from the training tasks to novel domains ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . Such positive cases, however, cannot establish transfer as a general rule. We ask the complementary question: when and why does RLVR generalization fail? However, we realize that such generalization of reasoning strategies has not been thoroughly investigated. Previous studies mostly understand RLVR generalization from its relationship with the base models ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) without clearly categorizing individual reasoning strategies and analyzing their OOD generalization. To this end, we start by building a controllable framework that clearly defines OOD generalization and categorizes reasoning strategies. As in Fig. 1 a , we construct a set of string functions f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) inspired by Yuan et al. (2026) , and let the LLM address this inverse problem: recovering multiple inputs x x such that f ⁡ ( x ) = y f(x)=y ( y y is a provided string output). This task mirrors solving math equations and tracing bugs in coding. More importantly, we construct the functions f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) f(\cdot) to be non-bijective and require LLMs to output k > 1 k>1 different solutions. This framework thus clearly splits in-distribution and OOD tasks, where the OOD tasks are built from held-out functions and made harder via longer strings y y and more required solutions k k . On this controllable framework, we observe that RLVR can reliably teach an LLM to perform reasoning effectively in-distribution , showing reliable derivation strategies step-by-step and enumerating characters only when needed, as Fig. 1 b . However, this model, named Mono , shows drastically different behaviors on harder OOD tasks: it abandons the strategy of derivation, and instead, relies on ineffective brute-force enumeration of all the digits simultaneously (Fig. 1 c ). Such an observation marks an important revelation: an LLM can learn to perform effective reasoning strategies in-distribution , yet drastically falls back to worse strategies in OOD scenarios . Such an observation is nuanced as it is not related to the commonly known RLVR failures like incapable base models or reward hacking, as the model is following valid reasoning traces to achieve high accuracy during training. Therefore, we are studying real generalization challenges under this setting. Figure 1: (a) To clearly define OOD generalization for LLM reasoning, we construct a controllable framework via solving string function equations, mirroring real-world math and coding. (b) We categorize two major reasoning strategies, the more effective Derivation and or total brute-force Enumeration . (c) We reveal how reasoning strategies reflect the challenges of OOD generalization. The Mono model learns derivation for ID cases, yet drastically collapses to enumeration for OOD. With Mixed better incentivizing the derivation strategy, it achieves much better OOD accuracy under similar ID performance. These form a systematic framework of understanding RLVR generalization. This diagnosis suggests that the key is not merely to improve training accuracy but to change which reasoning strategies RLVR incentivizes. We therefore introduce a seemingly indirect intervention for the task: co-training with bijective tasks that only asks for one solution x x for f ⁡ ( x ) = y f(x)=y . The intuition is to decrease the search space in non-bijective functions and encourage step-by-step derivation with larger certainties. Importantly, this intervention is surprising because the bijective tasks are not uniformly harder and are even further away from the non-bijective OOD evaluation requiring multiple solutions. Nevertheless, the Mixed model with this intervention successfully restores the behavior of utilizing the derivation strategy and leads to significantly better OOD accuracy (Fig. 1 c ). Such effectiveness inspires us to understand how better reasoning strategies can be incentivized from RLVR. As in Fig. 1 b , we view the reasoning process as progressively shrinking the candidate solution space. This analogy clearly distinguishes the derivation and enumeration: derivation is more effective by structurally pruning multiple candidates in a single step, while enumeration can only contribute marginally by eliminating one wrong candidate. Therefore, the reasoning strategies like derivation can contribute more bits per step, and can more easily generalize to harder scenarios, i.e. , those requiring more bits. So we Figure 3: Examples of reasoning strategies. start from categorizing the reasoning strategy utilized by the Mono model. As in Fig. 3 , we can clearly attribute two primary strategies: derivation , which structurally reverses f f and only conduct case-analysis when needed, and enumeration , which directly guess all the digits all at once, being much less efficient. To make this binary classification revealing the traits of reasoning strategies, we treat purely brute-force enumeration as “enumeration,” and everything else as “derivation.” In practice, we employ an LLM judge empowered by Gemini-3.0-Flash to classify the reasoning traces (clarification of our setup, details, and verification of LLM judge in Sec. B.1 ). From ID to OOD Collapse. Fig. 2(a) tracks accuracy during RL on the ID set and the four OOD sets, and Fig. 2(b) shows which strategies produce these responses. On in-distribution tasks, the Mono model learns the effective strategy of derivation in most cases and achieves high accuracy (as Fig. 2 , ID columns). However, its failure in OOD scenarios, e.g. , the novel functions of lenchange, is not solely due to longer reasoning or more computation. Rather, its reasoning skill of derivation acquired disappears on OOD tasks and gives way to the inefficient brute-force enumeration, which proposes all the digits of x x simultaneously, without utilizing the structure of the function f f . The majority of failures are caused by loops that enumerate all possible digits until reaching the token limits. Here, collapse refers to the reasoning strategy: Mono ’s derivation share drops from 85% on ID to below 50% on the three harder OOD sets. Accuracy, in contrast, degrades progressively as the shift grows: it stays above 80% on More Answers, the mildest shift, and drops to 6% on Length Change. Such an observation is surprising as it challenges RLVR generalization: the reasoning strategy already incentivized in RL fails to generalize despite identical task formats . As mentioned in Sec. 1 and Sec. 3 , this observation focuses on the meta-level reasoning skills of LLMs and is subtle and distinct from prior work. First, it is not a base-model limitation: the same model reaches ≈ 90 % \approx{}90\% on in-distribution non-bijective inversion. Second, it is not reward hacking : the LLM uses the correct and efficient derivation strategy for in-distribution evaluation rather than spurious shortcuts. We refer to this phenomenon as reasoning-strategy collapse , which motivates our central question: which training signal enables RLVR to generalize a reasoning pattern to OOD scenarios? Takeaway 1 Reasoning Strategy Collapse: Even though RLVR has incentivized the correct reasoning strategies for in-distribution tasks, the LLM might drastically change to ineffective strategies on OOD tasks despite identical task formats, undermining the generalization of RLVR. 4.2 Mixed Model: Enhancing OOD Generalization via Bijective Inversion The derivation reasoning strategy, avoiding pure enumeration, is thus our key to understanding RLVR generalization. Our intervention, therefore, is not to propose training tasks that are closer to the evaluation or simply harder than the existing training tasks, but a set of new tasks that more directly incentivize the derivation strategy. In fact, this is also why RLVR could bring improvements to multiple reasoning domains for LLMs in previous works ( Liu et al., 2026a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . Specifically, we propose using bijective functions as f f (both injective and surjective) to eliminate uncertainty in non-bijective tasks and encourage derivation via larger certainty. Enhancing OOD Generalization. Concretely, we co-train on bijective inversion with a 1 : 1 1{:}1 with the original non-bijective tasks, so this model is called Mixed . As shown in Fig. 2(b) , this almost doubles the utilization of derivation strategy compared with the Mono model, and leads to significantly better OOD evaluation (Fig. 2(a) ), especially on the novel functions of LenChange. Therefore, the incorporation of bijective inversion effectively improves the RLVR reasoning generalization. We have controlled the data recipe and training configuration for a fair comparison between the two models (details Sec. A.3 ) and additionally verified the main conclusions with multiple runs in Sec. B.2.4 .

items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.03625 (cs) [Submitted on 2 Nov 2026] Title: FADE: Factored Ability--Difficulty Filtering for Online RLVR Scheduling Authors: Tomas Duncun , Jonah Ellison , Mateo Ruiz , Hanae Fujita , Ingrid Solberg View a PDF of the paper titled FADE: Factored Ability--Difficulty Filtering for Online RLVR Scheduling, by Tomas Duncun and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) learns only from prompts whose sampled completions disagree: all-pass and all-fail groups produce zero relative advantage and burn generation budget without moving the policy. Adaptive schedulers try to steer rollouts toward informative prompts, yet they rely on per-prompt pass-rate trackers that entangle two quantities evolving at very different speeds---the policy's shifting competence across reasoning skills and each prompt's intrinsic difficulty. When a single exponential average or Beta counter tracks both at once, short memory scrambles the relative ordering of prompts whereas long memory reports stale pass rates. We introduce FADE (Factored Ability--Difficulty Estimation), a bilinear state-space filter that separates the two timescales. FADE represents each prompt's success logit as the inner product of a whitened $K$-dimensional skill loading with a fast-drifting policy ability vector, minus a slow-shrinking scalar item intercept. Using Pólya--Gamma augmentation, each minibatch of binary rollout outcomes updates the $K$-dimensional ability posterior in closed form via a rank-$K$ Woodbury step, instantly transferring competence shifts to all unobserved prompts that share those skills while leaving item intercepts stable. From the resulting posterior mean and variance we derive a closed-form utility for the probability of drawing a non-degenerate rollout group. Across five reasoning benchmarks, two base models, and four scheduling paradigms under a matched rollout budget, FADE consistently improves downstream accuracy and calibration while adding less than $0.6$\,ms per step. items.content: Fade : Factored Ability–Difficulty Filtering for Online RLVR Scheduling Tomas Duncun Affiliation: University of Michigan Jonah Ellison Affiliation: University of Michigan Mateo Ruiz Affiliation: University of Michigan Hanae Fujita Affiliation: University of Edinburgh Ingrid Solberg Affiliation: University of Edinburgh Abstract Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) learns only from prompts whose sampled completions disagree: all-pass and all-fail groups produce zero relative advantage and burn generation budget without moving the policy. Adaptive schedulers try to steer rollouts toward informative prompts, yet they rely on per-prompt pass-rate trackers that entangle two quantities evolving at very different speeds—the policy’s shifting competence across reasoning skills and each prompt’s intrinsic difficulty. When a single exponential average or Beta counter tracks both at once, short memory scrambles the relative ordering of prompts whereas long memory reports stale pass rates. We introduce Fade ( Factored Ability–Difficulty Estimation ), a bilinear state-space filter that separates the two timescales. Fade represents each prompt’s success logit as the inner product of a whitened K K -dimensional skill loading with a fast-drifting policy ability vector, minus a slow-shrinking scalar item intercept. Using Pólya–Gamma augmentation, each minibatch of binary rollout outcomes updates the K K -dimensional ability posterior in closed form via a rank- K K Woodbury step, instantly transferring competence shifts to all unobserved prompts that share those skills while leaving item intercepts stable. From the resulting posterior mean and variance we derive a closed-form utility for the probability of drawing a non-degenerate rollout group. Across five reasoning benchmarks, two base models, and four scheduling paradigms under a matched rollout budget, Fade consistently improves downstream accuracy and calibration while adding less than 0.6 0.6 ms per step. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) turns a rule-based answer checker into a policy improvement loop for mathematical and scientific reasoning ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Kimi Team et al., 2025 ) . Group-relative algorithms such as GRPO sample G G completions per prompt and standardize the binary rewards within each group ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . The bottleneck of this recipe is rollout generation, and its central pathology is group degeneracy : whenever a prompt is trivial for the current policy ( r i = 1 r_{i}{=}1 ) or far beyond its reach ( r i = 0 r_{i}{=}0 ), all G G completions receive the same reward, the group advantage vanishes, and the completions do no gradient work ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Yao et al., 2026a ; Mao et al., 2026b ) . Figure 1: Why per-prompt trackers face a coupling trade-off. (a) Along a GRPO run on NuminaMath, the absolute pass-rate level decorrelates within ∼ 100 {\sim}100 steps as the policy improves, whereas the relative difficulty ordering of prompts within a skill domain remains correlated over hundreds of steps. (b) Sweeping the decay rate of a per-prompt EMA traces a frontier between calibration error (Brier score) and rank correlation (Spearman ρ \rho ); per-item Bayesian trackers (DPS, CDAS) sit near that curve, whereas Fade decouples the two timescales. (c) Supplying factored estimates to a rollout scheduler sustains a higher fraction of non-zero advantage groups across the training budget. Adaptive RLVR schedulers attack group degeneracy from two angles. Curriculum selectors filter or prioritize prompts whose pass rate sits near the learning frontier ( Mao et al., 2026a ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Kong et al., 2026 ; Mao et al., 2026b ; Bae et al., 2026 ; Do et al., 2026 ) , while budget allocators vary the group size n i , t n_{i,t} per prompt to reduce gradient variance or maximize progress ( Yao et al., 2026a ; Nguyen et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Zou et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) . Both families need an online estimate of each prompt’s current pass probability p i , t p_{i,t} before rollouts are drawn. Existing trackers treat p i , t p_{i,t} as an unstructured per-prompt scalar and run into a fundamental dilemma. On-policy probing before each step is accurate but consumes tens of GPU-hours in extra generations ( Yao et al., 2026a ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Xu and Ding, 2025 ) , while small generalizable prompt predictive models ( Qu et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) require auxiliary model training and periodic recalibration. Zero-probe trackers instead smooth past training outcomes for each prompt via exponential moving averages, sliding windows, or dynamics-predictive Beta posteriors ( Mao et al., 2026a ; Kong et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Nguyen et al., 2026 ) . Because a corpus contains 10 5 10^{5} prompts and a batch touches only 256 256 , any individual prompt is revisited once every several hundred steps. Between visits, two things happen at very different speeds (Figure 1 (a)): the policy’s overall competence on a mathematical skill drifts quickly, while the fine-grained hardness gap between two problems requiring that skill barely moves. A single per-prompt memory parameter cannot serve both. Fast forgetting tracks recent pass rates on visited items but destroys the relative ranking of rarely visited items; slow forgetting preserves item ordering but reports badly lagging pass probabilities (Figure 1 (b)). We resolve this tension by factoring the logit of p i , t p_{i,t} into a low-rank dynamic policy state and a scalar static item intercept. Specifically, we project frozen prompt embeddings onto K K orthonormal whitened skill coordinates 𝐳 i ∈ ℝ K \mathbf{z}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} ( K = 32 K{=}32 ) and model the success logit at step t t as μ i , t = 𝐳 i ⊤ ​ 𝜽 t − b i \mu_{i,t}=\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\theta}_{t}-b_{i} . Here 𝜽 t ∈ ℝ K \bm{\theta}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} is a fast-evolving skill proficiency vector shared across the entire corpus, and b i ∈ ℝ b_{i}\in\mathbb{R} is a slow-shrinking intrinsic difficulty offset specific to prompt i i . Every minibatch of 256 256 prompts provides thousands of rollout outcomes that jointly pin down 𝜽 t \bm{\theta}_{t} ; updating 𝜽 t \bm{\theta}_{t} immediately shifts the predicted pass rate of all N N prompts in proportion to their skill loadings 𝐳 j \mathbf{z}_{j} , even if prompt j j has never been sampled. Meanwhile, b i b_{i} accumulates evidence over the full run with minimal forgetting, keeping within-skill prompt rankings sharp. To make inference exact and fast without inner optimization loops, Fade uses the Pólya–Gamma augmentation for binomial likelihoods ( Polson et al., 2013 ) . Conditioning on the local curvature parameter turns each step into a conjugate Gaussian Kalman update whose K × K K\times K covariance is maintained in 𝒪 ⁡ ( | B t | ​ K 2 ) \mathcal{O}(|B_{t}|K^{2}) time. Finally, rather than plugging point estimates into heuristic schedulers, we integrate the posterior uncertainty over the binomial group outcome to obtain a closed-form non-degenerate group utility 𝒰 i , t \mathcal{U}_{i,t} that directly scores the expected probability of drawing a mixed-reward group. Our contributions are three-fold: • We show that online difficulty estimation in RLVR is governed by two separated timescales—fast low-rank skill drift and slow item-level ordering—which single-timescale per-prompt trackers cannot simultaneously capture (§ 1 , § 3.2 ). • We propose Fade , a Pólya–Gamma bilinear state-space filter that updates a K K -dimensional skill state and per-item intercepts in closed form, paired with an uncertainty-calibrated non-degenerate group utility (§ 3 ). • We prove that Fade ’s Woodbury step is the exact conjugate mode under local Pólya–Gamma conditioning, that skill sharing strictly contracts predictive variance on unvisited prompts, and that factored filtering dominates single-memory trackers whenever skill drift exceeds item drift (§ 4 ). Across five math benchmarks and four schedulers, Fade consistently improves RLVR efficiency (§ 5 ). 2 Related Work Curriculum selection and rollout allocation in RLVR. Classical curriculum learning orders examples by difficulty or learnability ( Bengio et al., 2009 ; Mindermann et al., 2022 ) . In group-relative RLVR ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) , prompts whose completions all succeed or all fail yield zero advantage, motivating group-prioritized optimization that eliminates ineffective samples ( Mao et al., 2026b ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . Recent selectors therefore filter or reweight prompts using dynamics-predictive sampling ( Mao et al., 2026a ) , lightweight prompt predictive models ( Qu et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) , competence gaps, or reward dynamics ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Kong et al., 2026 ; Bae et al., 2026 ; Do et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Zhang and Zuo, 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Lai and Nissim, 2026 ; Jia et al., 2026 ; Pant et al., 2026 ) . A parallel line allocates non-uniform rollout budgets n i , t n_{i,t} across a batch to minimize policy-gradient variance ( Yao et al., 2026a ; Nguyen et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) , unify budget allocation across reasoning and agentic RL ( Zou et al., 2026 ) , or maximize sequential utility ( Xiong et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Yao et al., 2026b ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026b ; Kalarde et al., 2026 ) . Complementary work prunes partial trajectories or rescales advantages ( Xu et al., 2026a ; Xia et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026c ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Dao et al., 2026 ; Son et al., 2026 ; Gholipour et al., 2026 ) . All of these schedulers consume an online pass-rate estimate; Fade replaces that estimator without altering the downstream scheduling rule. Dynamic difficulty tracking and Item Response Theory. Static item response theory (IRT) separates model ability from item difficulty in offline NLP evaluation ( Lalor et al., 2016 ; Rodriguez et al., 2021 ) . During RLVR, however, the policy moves at every step ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . Probing methods estimate current pass rates via extra on-policy rollouts ( Yao et al., 2026a ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Xu and Ding, 2025 ) , trading compute for freshness. Amortized predictive models estimate prompt utility or difficulty from text features ( Qu et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) , offering strong zero-shot generalization when paired with online adaptation. History-based trackers update per-prompt statistics from training rollouts—via dynamics-predictive Beta-Binomial filtering in DPS ( Mao et al., 2026a ) , historical discrepancy ( Kong et al., 2026 ) , reward regularity ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , or local regression ( Nguyen et al., 2026 ) —while unified rollout trackers ( Zou et al., 2026 ) , offline tree structures ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , bandit curricula ( Xu et al., 2026b ) , and lag-corrected replay ( Mao et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026d ) address related aspects of non-stationarity. Fade brings multidimensional IRT online via Pólya–Gamma filtering ( Polson et al., 2013 ) , separating fast low-rank skill evolution from static item hardness. 3 Method Figure 2: Fade architecture. (A) Offline, frozen prompt representations are whitened into K K orthogonal skill loadings 𝐳 i ∈ ℝ K \mathbf{z}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} and an initial difficulty offset b ^ i , 0 \hat{b}_{i,0} . (B) Online, a dual-timescale Pólya–Gamma filter updates the fast policy skill state 𝜽 t ∈ ℝ K \bm{\theta}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} (forgetting ρ \rho ) via a rank- K K Woodbury step and refines the slow item intercept b i b_{i} (forgetting γ b ≈ 1 \gamma_{b}{\approx}1 ). Changes in 𝜽 ^ t \hat{\bm{\theta}}_{t} immediately update all N N prompts sharing those skills. (C) The posterior mean and variance define the expected non-degenerate group utility 𝒰 i , t \mathcal{U}_{i,t} for prompt selection and rollout allocation. 3.1 Setup and Group Degeneracy Consider a prompt pool 𝒟 = { x i } i = 1 N \mathcal{D}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} . At training step t t , the scheduler selects a minibatch ℬ t ⊂ 𝒟 \mathcal{B}_{t}\subset\mathcal{D} and allocates n i , t n_{i,t} rollouts to each i ∈ ℬ t i\in\mathcal{B}_{t} under policy π t \pi_{t} . A deterministic verifier scores each completion y i , t , g ∈ { 0 , 1 } y_{i,t,g}\in\{0,1\} , yielding s i , t = ∑ g = 1 n i , t y i , t , g s_{i,t}=\sum_{g=1}^{n_{i,t}}y_{i,t,g} successes and empirical pass rate r i , t = s i , t / n i , t r_{i,t}=s_{i,t}/n_{i,t} . items.raw_text: Fade : Factored Ability–Difficulty Filtering for Online RLVR Scheduling Tomas Duncun Affiliation: University of Michigan Jonah Ellison Affiliation: University of Michigan Mateo Ruiz Affiliation: University of Michigan Hanae Fujita Affiliation: University of Edinburgh Ingrid Solberg Affiliation: University of Edinburgh Abstract Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) learns only from prompts whose sampled completions disagree: all-pass and all-fail groups produce zero relative advantage and burn generation budget without moving the policy. Adaptive schedulers try to steer rollouts toward informative prompts, yet they rely on per-prompt pass-rate trackers that entangle two quantities evolving at very different speeds—the policy’s shifting competence across reasoning skills and each prompt’s intrinsic difficulty. When a single exponential average or Beta counter tracks both at once, short memory scrambles the relative ordering of prompts whereas long memory reports stale pass rates. We introduce Fade ( Factored Ability–Difficulty Estimation ), a bilinear state-space filter that separates the two timescales. Fade represents each prompt’s success logit as the inner product of a whitened K K -dimensional skill loading with a fast-drifting policy ability vector, minus a slow-shrinking scalar item intercept. Using Pólya–Gamma augmentation, each minibatch of binary rollout outcomes updates the K K -dimensional ability posterior in closed form via a rank- K K Woodbury step, instantly transferring competence shifts to all unobserved prompts that share those skills while leaving item intercepts stable. From the resulting posterior mean and variance we derive a closed-form utility for the probability of drawing a non-degenerate rollout group. Across five reasoning benchmarks, two base models, and four scheduling paradigms under a matched rollout budget, Fade consistently improves downstream accuracy and calibration while adding less than 0.6 0.6 ms per step. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) turns a rule-based answer checker into a policy improvement loop for mathematical and scientific reasoning ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Kimi Team et al., 2025 ) . Group-relative algorithms such as GRPO sample G G completions per prompt and standardize the binary rewards within each group ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . The bottleneck of this recipe is rollout generation, and its central pathology is group degeneracy : whenever a prompt is trivial for the current policy ( r i = 1 r_{i}{=}1 ) or far beyond its reach ( r i = 0 r_{i}{=}0 ), all G G completions receive the same reward, the group advantage vanishes, and the completions do no gradient work ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Yao et al., 2026a ; Mao et al., 2026b ) . Figure 1: Why per-prompt trackers face a coupling trade-off. (a) Along a GRPO run on NuminaMath, the absolute pass-rate level decorrelates within ∼ 100 {\sim}100 steps as the policy improves, whereas the relative difficulty ordering of prompts within a skill domain remains correlated over hundreds of steps. (b) Sweeping the decay rate of a per-prompt EMA traces a frontier between calibration error (Brier score) and rank correlation (Spearman ρ \rho ); per-item Bayesian trackers (DPS, CDAS) sit near that curve, whereas Fade decouples the two timescales. (c) Supplying factored estimates to a rollout scheduler sustains a higher fraction of non-zero advantage groups across the training budget. Adaptive RLVR schedulers attack group degeneracy from two angles. Curriculum selectors filter or prioritize prompts whose pass rate sits near the learning frontier ( Mao et al., 2026a ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Kong et al., 2026 ; Mao et al., 2026b ; Bae et al., 2026 ; Do et al., 2026 ) , while budget allocators vary the group size n i , t n_{i,t} per prompt to reduce gradient variance or maximize progress ( Yao et al., 2026a ; Nguyen et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Zou et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) . Both families need an online estimate of each prompt’s current pass probability p i , t p_{i,t} before rollouts are drawn. Existing trackers treat p i , t p_{i,t} as an unstructured per-prompt scalar and run into a fundamental dilemma. On-policy probing before each step is accurate but consumes tens of GPU-hours in extra generations ( Yao et al., 2026a ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Xu and Ding, 2025 ) , while small generalizable prompt predictive models ( Qu et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) require auxiliary model training and periodic recalibration. Zero-probe trackers instead smooth past training outcomes for each prompt via exponential moving averages, sliding windows, or dynamics-predictive Beta posteriors ( Mao et al., 2026a ; Kong et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Nguyen et al., 2026 ) . Because a corpus contains 10 5 10^{5} prompts and a batch touches only 256 256 , any individual prompt is revisited once every several hundred steps. Between visits, two things happen at very different speeds (Figure 1 (a)): the policy’s overall competence on a mathematical skill drifts quickly, while the fine-grained hardness gap between two problems requiring that skill barely moves. A single per-prompt memory parameter cannot serve both. Fast forgetting tracks recent pass rates on visited items but destroys the relative ranking of rarely visited items; slow forgetting preserves item ordering but reports badly lagging pass probabilities (Figure 1 (b)). We resolve this tension by factoring the logit of p i , t p_{i,t} into a low-rank dynamic policy state and a scalar static item intercept. Specifically, we project frozen prompt embeddings onto K K orthonormal whitened skill coordinates 𝐳 i ∈ ℝ K \mathbf{z}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} ( K = 32 K{=}32 ) and model the success logit at step t t as μ i , t = 𝐳 i ⊤ ​ 𝜽 t − b i \mu_{i,t}=\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\theta}_{t}-b_{i} . Here 𝜽 t ∈ ℝ K \bm{\theta}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} is a fast-evolving skill proficiency vector shared across the entire corpus, and b i ∈ ℝ b_{i}\in\mathbb{R} is a slow-shrinking intrinsic difficulty offset specific to prompt i i . Every minibatch of 256 256 prompts provides thousands of rollout outcomes that jointly pin down 𝜽 t \bm{\theta}_{t} ; updating 𝜽 t \bm{\theta}_{t} immediately shifts the predicted pass rate of all N N prompts in proportion to their skill loadings 𝐳 j \mathbf{z}_{j} , even if prompt j j has never been sampled. Meanwhile, b i b_{i} accumulates evidence over the full run with minimal forgetting, keeping within-skill prompt rankings sharp. To make inference exact and fast without inner optimization loops, Fade uses the Pólya–Gamma augmentation for binomial likelihoods ( Polson et al., 2013 ) . Conditioning on the local curvature parameter turns each step into a conjugate Gaussian Kalman update whose K × K K\times K covariance is maintained in 𝒪 ⁡ ( | B t | ​ K 2 ) \mathcal{O}(|B_{t}|K^{2}) time. Finally, rather than plugging point estimates into heuristic schedulers, we integrate the posterior uncertainty over the binomial group outcome to obtain a closed-form non-degenerate group utility 𝒰 i , t \mathcal{U}_{i,t} that directly scores the expected probability of drawing a mixed-reward group. Our contributions are three-fold: • We show that online difficulty estimation in RLVR is governed by two separated timescales—fast low-rank skill drift and slow item-level ordering—which single-timescale per-prompt trackers cannot simultaneously capture (§ 1 , § 3.2 ). • We propose Fade , a Pólya–Gamma bilinear state-space filter that updates a K K -dimensional skill state and per-item intercepts in closed form, paired with an uncertainty-calibrated non-degenerate group utility (§ 3 ). • We prove that Fade ’s Woodbury step is the exact conjugate mode under local Pólya–Gamma conditioning, that skill sharing strictly contracts predictive variance on unvisited prompts, and that factored filtering dominates single-memory trackers whenever skill drift exceeds item drift (§ 4 ). Across five math benchmarks and four schedulers, Fade consistently improves RLVR efficiency (§ 5 ). 2 Related Work Curriculum selection and rollout allocation in RLVR. Classical curriculum learning orders examples by difficulty or learnability ( Bengio et al., 2009 ; Mindermann et al., 2022 ) . In group-relative RLVR ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) , prompts whose completions all succeed or all fail yield zero advantage, motivating group-prioritized optimization that eliminates ineffective samples ( Mao et al., 2026b ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . Recent selectors therefore filter or reweight prompts using dynamics-predictive sampling ( Mao et al., 2026a ) , lightweight prompt predictive models ( Qu et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) , competence gaps, or reward dynamics ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Kong et al., 2026 ; Bae et al., 2026 ; Do et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Zhang and Zuo, 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Lai and Nissim, 2026 ; Jia et al., 2026 ; Pant et al., 2026 ) . A parallel line allocates non-uniform rollout budgets n i , t n_{i,t} across a batch to minimize policy-gradient variance ( Yao et al., 2026a ; Nguyen et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) , unify budget allocation across reasoning and agentic RL ( Zou et al., 2026 ) , or maximize sequential utility ( Xiong et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Yao et al., 2026b ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026b ; Kalarde et al., 2026 ) . Complementary work prunes partial trajectories or rescales advantages ( Xu et al., 2026a ; Xia et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026c ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Dao et al., 2026 ; Son et al., 2026 ; Gholipour et al., 2026 ) . All of these schedulers consume an online pass-rate estimate; Fade replaces that estimator without altering the downstream scheduling rule. Dynamic difficulty tracking and Item Response Theory. Static item response theory (IRT) separates model ability from item difficulty in offline NLP evaluation ( Lalor et al., 2016 ; Rodriguez et al., 2021 ) . During RLVR, however, the policy moves at every step ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . Probing methods estimate current pass rates via extra on-policy rollouts ( Yao et al., 2026a ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Xu and Ding, 2025 ) , trading compute for freshness. Amortized predictive models estimate prompt utility or difficulty from text features ( Qu et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) , offering strong zero-shot generalization when paired with online adaptation. History-based trackers update per-prompt statistics from training rollouts—via dynamics-predictive Beta-Binomial filtering in DPS ( Mao et al., 2026a ) , historical discrepancy ( Kong et al., 2026 ) , reward regularity ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , or local regression ( Nguyen et al., 2026 ) —while unified rollout trackers ( Zou et al., 2026 ) , offline tree structures ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , bandit curricula ( Xu et al., 2026b ) , and lag-corrected replay ( Mao et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026d ) address related aspects of non-stationarity. Fade brings multidimensional IRT online via Pólya–Gamma filtering ( Polson et al., 2013 ) , separating fast low-rank skill evolution from static item hardness. 3 Method Figure 2: Fade architecture. (B) Online, a dual-timescale Pólya–Gamma filter updates the fast policy skill state 𝜽 t ∈ ℝ K \bm{\theta}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} (forgetting ρ \rho ) via a rank- K K Woodbury step and refines the slow item intercept b i b_{i} (forgetting γ b ≈ 1 \gamma_{b}{\approx}1 ). items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.03623 (cs) [Submitted on 2 Nov 2026] Title: Thought-deciphering via hierarchical EEG-to-text alignment Authors: Xiaopeng Mao , Morten Mørup , Xin Xu , Sang Wan Lee , Sadasivan Puthusserypady View a PDF of the paper titled Thought-deciphering via hierarchical EEG-to-text alignment, by Xiaopeng Mao and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Communication is important for our well-being, but it can be impaired by disabilities, such as locked-in syndrome (LIS), cerebral palsy (CP), and dysarthria. Non-invasive brain-to-text brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer a promising solution by providing an alternative communication pathway for people with communication disabilities. However, most recent breakthroughs have relied on large, cumbersome, and costly neuroimaging modalities, such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). Numerous studies have attempted decoding using the lighter and cheaper electroencephalography (EEG), but the results remain inferior compared to the other modalities. More importantly, we do not understand how these modalities are related to text at the letter, word, sentence, and higher semantic levels. Many prior studies have focused on decoding below the sentence level because it is considerably easier to design an experiment around phonemes, letters, and words. However, during communication, sentences play a much more important role than words and letters. This is because sentences carry information at such a high level that they can be understood even if some words and letters are missing. However, within sentence-level decoding, sentence classification is not as well investigated as sentence generation, making it difficult to decide whether a sentence should be retrieved or generated in the context of EEG-to-text decoding. This paper strives to investigate sentence-level EEG-to-text classification via a novel hierarchical alignment framework, where the main goal is to retrieve a read sentence using its context and EEG as inputs. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.03641 (cs) [Submitted on 2 Nov 2026] Title: From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles Authors: Paulius Skaisgiris , Thomas Pammer , Veronika Semmelrock , Mykyta Ielanskyi , Maximilian Heisinger , Erich Kobler View a PDF of the paper titled From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles, by Paulius Skaisgiris and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation has substantially improved the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, including code generation, data analysis, and exam-style question answering. Despite these advances, purely neural LLMs continue to struggle with elementary logical reasoning problems and lack the determinism, soundness, and reliability characteristic of symbolic reasoning systems. Conversely, classical symbolic methods such as SAT solving and exact cover guarantee correctness and completeness, but require problems to be expressed in highly specialized formal encodings, limiting their applicability to natural language inputs. In this work, we present a synergistic neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by combining neural semantic parsing with deterministic exact cover reasoning. Given a Zebra-style logic puzzle in natural language, an LLM translates entities and constraints into structured tool calls that construct an exact cover instance. A symbolic solver then computes the solution and provides feedback to iteratively refine invalid, under- or overconstrained encodings, exploiting the uniqueness property of Zebra puzzles. We conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple parameter scales, post-training paradigms, and LLM families. The results demonstrate that our hybrid approach consistently outperforms strong plain neural baselines, including CoT prompting, as well as recent neuro-symbolic methods. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.03634 (cs) [Submitted on 2 Nov 2026] Title: WebHarbor: Docking Real Websites for Evolving GUI Agent Environments Authors: Zhaoyang Wang , Qianhui Wu , Boyu Gou , Demi Wang , Jiacheng Zhang , Peichun Hua , Qize Li , Shi Qiu , Yifan Jiang , Yifan Zhang , Zexu Jin , Baolin Peng , Bolin Shen , Chetan Bansal , Dehan Kong , Deren Lei , Dongshen Peng , Fengqing Jiang , Hao Cheng , Haoqing Wang , Jiaming Shan , Jicheng Wang , Jingguang Zhou , Jixuan He , Kaide Zeng , Kangyu Zhu , Lama Moukheiber , Mufan Qiu , Peng Xia , Qihan Sun , Qingwei Lin , Qiushi Sun , Ruichen Zhang , Shuqing Luo , Si Qin , Sicheng Fan , Tao Xiong , Wenlin Yao , Xinyu Zhang , Xinyue Zeng , Xuanrui Li , Xuchao Zhang , Yian Wang , Yichao Liu , Yiming Liang , Yiyang Zhou , Yizhu Jiao , Yuetai Li , Yurun Chen , Yuxuan Zhang , Zheyuan Yang , Zhiyuan Yao , Zhongyang Li , Zihao Li , Zili Wang , Jianfeng Gao , Huaxiu Yao View a PDF of the paper titled WebHarbor: Docking Real Websites for Evolving GUI Agent Environments, by Zhaoyang Wang and 56 other authors View PDF Abstract: GUI web agents require realistic and interactive environments that remain stable during both evaluation and training. Live website evaluation suffers from changing content, access restrictions, and limited coverage of authenticated workflows, while existing synthetic environments for training often lack functional depth and visual fidelity. We propose WebHarbor, a suite of 153 executable and dockerized website environments that faithfully reconstruct the visual interfaces, content, and functional workflows of real-world web services under deterministic control. We build WebHarbor through task-driven human-agent collaboration, where environments evolve as new tasks expand their functional scope, coding agents implement the required changes, and human contributors audit visual fidelity, functional correctness, and task validity. The resulting suite comprises 3,518 tasks spanning multi-step and post-authentication workflows, where existing works often fail to cover. Beyond reliable evaluation, WebHarbor provides high-fidelity synthetic web environments for cost-efficient reinforcement learning (RL). We demonstrate that a Qwen 4B-level GUI agent trained with RL in WebHarbor generalizes to unseen tasks and performs competitively with leading open-source GUI web agents across four benchmarks. The code and data are publicly available at this https URL . items.summary: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.03618 (cs) [Submitted on 2 Nov 2026] Title: Strategist: Evolving Reasoning with Agents Authors: Taiming Lu , Qi Xu , Zhigang Hua , Zhuang Liu View a PDF of the paper titled Strategist: Evolving Reasoning with Agents, by Taiming Lu and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: A model is only half of an AI agent system. The other half is the inference strategy: the reasoning procedure that turns model calls into a response. Today that second half is written by hand, and the experience of building one strategy never carries to the next. We introduce Strategist, a meta-agent that evolves inference strategies across tasks. Each strategy is written as a blueprint,executable code that other strategies can reuse, and together the blueprints form a library. Given a task and a small development set, Strategist retrieves related blueprints, writes candidate strategies, tests them on real samples, and revises them from the results

items.content: Strategist : Evolving Reasoning with Agents Taiming Lu 1 Qi Xu 2 Zhigang Hua 2 Zhuang Liu 1 1 Princeton University 2 Meta Abstract A model is only half of an AI agent system. The other half is the inference strategy: the reasoning procedure that turns model calls into a response. Today that second half is written by hand, and the experience of building one strategy never carries to the next. We introduce Strategist , a meta-agent that evolves inference strategies across tasks. Each strategy is written as a blueprint, executable code that other strategies can reuse, and together the blueprints form a library. Given a task and a small development set, Strategist retrieves related blueprints, writes candidate strategies, tests them on real samples, and revises them from the results. Every candidate then enters the library, so later tasks build on earlier discoveries. On 30 benchmarks, Strategist beats the strongest baseline on 24 and matches its average accuracy ( 74.7 % 74.7\% vs. 74.0 % 74.0\% ) at 39% lower inference cost. Its strategies also transfer to unseen tasks and other models without further search. The part of an AI system that is not improved on its own now does. Code Figure 1 : Strategist turns strategy design into a search that accumulates knowledge. Top: in each round, an LLM writes new inference strategies as code, runs them, and stores every one, with its measured accuracy and cost, in a library shared across tasks, so later tasks build on what earlier ones found. The models stay frozen; only the strategies change. Bottom: the search matches the strongest baseline (BL) at lower cost, and its strategies work on new tasks and new models without further search. Cost ratios are per-benchmark averages; transfer costs are totals in USD. Section 1 Introduction Figure 2 : Strategy design is per task; Strategist makes it cumulative. By hand and in prior automated search, nothing carries between tasks. Strategist keeps every strategy in a library that the next task starts from. A model is only half of an AI system. The other half is how that model is put to work, and it matters just as much. Everything from the prompt to the reasoning procedure decides how it behaves. Today that second half is designed by people, fixed, one system at a time. Someone writes the prompt, tries it, adjusts it, and once the system works, the design is left as it is. It is the part of the system that never improves on its own. There is no reason it has to stay that way. The prompts and reasoning procedures that put a model to work are text and code, and agents themselves have become good at writing both. What humans do to design (write, try, adjust) such inference strategies is the natural agentic loop. Such loops have already been shown to evolve programs far beyond their starting point ( Novikov et al., 2025 ) , and AI scientists now run the same loop end to end ( Lu et al., 2024 ; Gottweis et al., 2025 ; Yamada et al., 2025 ) . Designing an inference strategy is the same work with a different object. So why not evolve agentic reasoning itself the same way? Run on far more cases than a person could try, the loop could outdo what people build by hand. Recent work has begun to automate this loop: searching over strategy designs, as raw code or as assemblies of fixed components ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ; Shang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) ; training controllers that route each input to an existing strategy ( Taparia et al., 2026 ; Yue et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Su et al., 2025 ) ; or optimizing one strategy per task by training, evolution, or iterative refinement ( Gao et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) . All of them beat hand-designed strategies on individual benchmarks, and all of them stop there. Searching or routing over a fixed set of strategies can never discover a new one. Trained optimizers need to start over for every task. These methods make the design automatic. We want to make it cumulative (Figure 2 ). We start from the representation. Evolving strategies needs a form open enough to express any reasoning procedure and structured enough for later searches to reuse and combine. We introduce the Strategy Blueprint : an executable program with one shared code interface, so any blueprint can serve as a component inside another. New designs are built from old ones, and the library grows as it is used. On this representation we build Strategist , a meta-agent that does not answer questions but designs the strategies that do. It runs the write, try, adjust loop at scale, with frozen models and no training. Given a task and a small development set, it writes candidate strategies as blueprints, runs them on real samples, reads the traces, and revises them against measured accuracy and cost. Before each round it queries a shared library for relevant blueprints and for diverse ones as inspiration. After each round every candidate goes back into the library with its measurements and experience notes. On 30 benchmarks spanning math, code, commonsense, multi-hop QA, knowledge, logic, and recommendation, we compare Strategist against 18 baselines. Strategist wins on 24 of 30, matching the strongest baseline’s average accuracy ( 74.0 % → 74.7 % 74.0\%\!\to\!74.7\% ) at 39% lower cost. The library pays off on its own: on 10 held-out benchmarks, retrieval with no search stays within 2 points of the strongest baseline on all 10 and beats it on 8 ( 77.8 % → 81.4 % 77.8\%\to 81.4\% ). The same strategies, moved to GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5 without changing a line, still beat the baselines there. Each task solved leaves the next one a better place to start. Until now, only the model in an AI system could learn. Now the rest of it can too. Figure 3 : The Strategy Blueprint is a freeform graph that grows through the library. (a) Two foundations ( chat and agent ) sit at the top. Strategies compose from them and from each other, forming a directed graph whose levels emerge naturally from composition depth. (b) Four protocols govern the graph: every node shares one abstract interface, each node can only call nodes created before it, no cycles are allowed, and no duplicates should exist. Section 2 The Strategy Blueprint Every inference strategy, ultimately, is a program. How it is represented determines what an automated designer can build, test, and reuse. Existing work represents strategies as computation graphs ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Zhuge et al., 2024 ) and declarative pipelines ( Khattab et al., 2024 ; Yue et al., 2026 ) , which are composable but can only express pre-defined patterns, or as monolithic code ( Hu et al., 2025 ) , which can express anything but produces isolated strategies. We introduce the Strategy Blueprint : a reasoning flow that specifies how to solve a task (which models to call, in what order, at which tier, and how) using the open interface of code. Every blueprint exposes the same interface, so any can call any other, and a library can grow by composition. Figure 4 : Strategy blueprint captures reasoning structure. This simplified blueprint example defines the steps, control flow, and the model tier for each step. Prompts are not specified; filling in produces a runnable strategy. Foundations. A blueprint is a Python program that captures the structure of a reasoning strategy without the task-specific prompts. For example, one blueprint defines a loop: generate three candidate answers, review each, then majority-vote. Filling in prompts produces a runnable strategy . It has one interface, execute(llm, task) -> str , and is built from two foundations: chat (single- or multi-turn conversation) and agent (with scaffold and tools). See Figure 4 for an example. Multi-tier model routing. We allow strategies to route across three model tiers ( fast , balanced , complex ), each in two modes ( nothink and thinking ), mirroring the tiered pricing and effort levels of common model providers. Not every reasoning step needs the same intelligence, so each step can target a different tier. This internal routing is what allows a single strategy to be accurate and cost-efficient at the same time. The Blueprint Library. Blueprints live in a shared library that grows over time. They are added along with their measured performance and experience notes on when it works and when it does not. Because every blueprint exposes the same interface, a new blueprint can use any existing one as a component, so the library compounds: early blueprints build on the two foundations, later ones compose from those, and depth grows naturally (Figure 3 a ). Four protocols govern the library (Figure 3 b ): a shared interface, no forward calls, no cycles, and no duplicates. Figure 5 : The Strategist four-stage iterative pipeline. Each iteration: (1) Retrieve relevant blueprints and diverse inspiration from the Library; (2) Propose K K candidates as a mix of new , composed , and reuse blueprints paired with task-specific prompts; (3) Evaluate each candidate, seeing full traces on the training set and aggregated scores on validation; (4) Accumulate the underlying blueprints into the library with measurement cards and experience notes. Section 3 Strategist Given a task and a small development set, Strategist iteratively retrieves relevant blueprints, proposes K = 5 K{=}5 candidates, evaluates them on real samples, and accumulates the results back into the library (Figure 5 ). After N N iterations, the candidate that beats BL on both the validation and hidden splits by the largest hidden-set margin is returned, or BL itself if none does (Algorithm 1 ). Step 1: Retrieve. The strategist queries the Blueprint Library with a short text prompt. The search is hybrid (TF–IDF plus embedding similarity). Each blueprint carries traits, a measurement card, and experience notes written by previous strategists; the search indexes over all of these, so the strategist finds blueprints by measured behavior and prior analyses, not just structural similarity. Beyond relevant results, the library returns adjacent inspiration (blueprints from other domains or reasoning patterns) to inspire new designs. Step 2: Propose. Using the retrieved blueprints and inspiration, the strategist designs new blueprints or composes from existing ones, each paired with task-specific prompts to form candidate strategies. Each blueprint must be one of three kinds: new (a blueprint with no library backbone), composed (a blueprint that wraps or extends an existing one), or reuse (directly applies an existing library blueprint with new prompts). Every iteration includes at least one candidate of each kind, balancing exploration and exploitation. Step 3: Evaluate. The system operates at two levels. At the agent level (inner loop), each candidate strategy processes inputs directly, and the strategist observes the full reasoning trace, execution status, and scores. At the meta level (outer loop), the strategist uses these observations to improve its proposals. The data is split into four parts. The training set : strategies run on these samples and the strategist sees both the scores and the full agent traces. The validation set : strategies also run on these samples, but the strategist sees only the aggregated scores; this mirrors standard train/validation practice and prevents overfitting to the training signal. The hidden set : used to select the winning strategy across all iterations, preventing overfitting to any single iteration. The test set : held out entirely from the search loop and used only for final confirmation. Step 4: Accumulate. The library stores blueprints, not strategies: it retains the reusable structure while discarding task-specific prompts. This is what enables cross-task transfer. After each iteration, the strategist writes an analysis of each candidate’s structural properties and adds the underlying blueprints to the library with their measurement cards and experience notes, with deduplication. Section 4 Experiments Benchmarks. We evaluate on 40 benchmarks spanning seven categories (Table 2 ). From these, 30 randomly selected benchmarks form the main results and 10 are held out for one-shot retrieval. Each benchmark is split into training, validation, and hidden sets of up to 100 samples each, plus a fixed 200-sample test set. We randomly select 30 for the main iterative search and hold out the remaining 10 for one-shot retrieval. Each benchmark is split into training, validation, hidden, and test sets. Prompting Monte-Carlo vote Chain-of-thought ( Wei et al., 2022 ) Self-discover ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) Direct thinking Tree of thoughts ( Yao et al., 2023a ) Self-refine ( Madaan et al., 2023 ) Shortlist vote Self-consistency ( Wang et al., 2023 ) Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) Direct Least-to-most ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) CoVe ( Dhuliawala et al., 2024 ) Agentic Agent with code Multi-agent debate ( Du et al., 2024 ) MetaGPT ( Hong et al., 2024 ) Vanilla agent Chain-of-agents ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) AutoGen ( Wu et al., 2023 ) Table 2 : Baselines. Prompting methods call the model directly; agentic methods add tool use or multiple interacting agents. Each baseline runs at all six tier/mode configurations, and we compare against the strongest training split cell. Models. The task models consist of three tiers: Qwen3-0.6B (fast), Qwen3-1.7B (balanced), and Qwen3-4B (complex), each run with thinking off (nothink) or on (thinking), giving six model configs. The strategist is GPT-6, a separate frozen LLM accessed through the Codex CLI; it writes strategies but never answers questions. Baselines. We compare against 18 baselines (Table 2 ), all using the same task models without internet access. They span from direct prompting to multi-agent workflows, and each runs at all six model configurations, giving 18 × 6 = 108 18\times 6=108 cells per benchmark. Our baseline (BL) is the cell most accurate on a benchmark’s training split, scored on the test set. This mirrors deployment: a method is chosen on the small sample at hand, then applied to a larger unseen sample from the same distribution. Our strategy is likewise chosen without seeing the test set. Metrics. We report accuracy and weighted cost. Cost is token usage (input and output) weighted by tier (fast = 1 × =1\times , balanced = 2.83 × =2.83\times , complex = 6.67 × =6.67\times , matching the 0.6B/1.7B/4B parameter ratio), since per-token floating-point operations (FLOPs) scale linearly with the parameter count ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ) . Figure 6 : Ours among all 108 baseline cells (accuracy vs weighted cost per sample, test set). Each small marker is one baseline cell (a baseline strategy at one model tier and mode); the star is Strategist ’s strategy. BL, the comparison point, is the cell chosen on the training split (Figure 7 ). The highest marker in a panel is the best of 108 cells chosen by looking at the test results , which no method can do in advance; it is shown for context, not as the comparison point. Appendix Figure 10 shows the same view on the training split, where the bias runs the other way. Against BL, Ours is more than 2% cheaper on 26 of 30 benchmarks and within 2 accuracy points or better on 28. Figure 7 : Per-benchmark head-to-head: Strategist vs the baseline (BL) on the 30 main benchmarks. For each benchmark, test accuracy (%, left axis) and weighted cost per sample (log scale, right axis) of Ours and of BL. BL is the baseline cell (one of the 18 × 6 18\times 6 baseline–configuration pairs) that is most accurate on the benchmark’s training split, scored on the test set; Strategist ’s strategy is also chosen without seeing the test set, so this is the like-for-like comparison behind the win counts. Numbers above each pair are relative changes (green: improvement; grey: regression under 2%; orange: larger regression). Section 5 Results We run the full Strategist loop on each of the 30 main benchmarks. BL is the cell of the 18 × 6 18\times 6 baseline matrix that is most accurate on the benchmark’s training split; all methods share the same executors, extractor, and 200-sample test split. A strategy wins if it is better than BL on accuracy (by more than 2 points) or on cost (by more than 2%) and worse on neither. Strategist wins on 24 of 30 benchmarks, ties on 2 (MBPP+, MinervaM), trades accuracy for cost on 2 (MedQA, AIME) and loses on 2 (HotpotQA and COPA, at equal accuracy but 9% and 6% higher cost); it cuts weighted cost by more than 2% on 26 of 30 (Figure 7 ; Figure 6 places Ours among all 108 baseline cells; per-benchmark numbers in Appendix C.1 ). On average, Strategist matches BL’s accuracy ( 74.0 % → 74.7 % 74.0\%\to 74.7\% ) while reducing weighted cost by 39 % 39\% (a mean per-benchmark cost ratio of 0.61 × 0.61\times relative to BL). The largest accuracy gains come with large cost cuts: SQuAD v2 ( 73.2 % → 79.1 % 73.2\%\to 79.1\% at 0.23 × 0.23\times cost), TruthfulQA ( + 4.5 +4.5 points), 2WikiMQA ( + 4.0 +4.0 at 0.34 × 0.34\times ), Amazon-Rec ( + 4.0 +4.0 ), SAT-Math ( + 3.6 +3.6 at 0.41 × 0.41\times ), LSAT-AR ( + 3.4 +3.4 ) and LSAT-RC ( + 3.0 +3.0 at 0.50 × 0.50\times ). On benchmarks where the models are near their accuracy ceiling (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K, ASDiv, SciQ, MMLU-STEM-Hard), Strategist keeps accuracy within 2 points of BL and cuts cost instead, by 66–89%. Of the 24 wins, most come from strategist-designed strategies and and some are from simpler baseline scripts, found during search, that match BL’s accuracy at a lower cost. Strategist is not Pareto-improving everywhere: on MedQA and AIME 2024 it is cheaper ( 0.44 × 0.44\times , 0.77 × 0.77\times ) but 4–5 points less accurate, and on HotpotQA and COPA it matches accuracy at slightly higher cost. One-shot library retrieval. The 30-benchmark main run grew the library to 1,865 1{,}865 blueprints. We test if a future task can skip the full search: on 10 held-out benchmarks, the strategist queries the final strategies of the main searches (not the full library) once, instantiates the top-5 retrieved blueprints for the task, measures each on up to 300 development questions, and runs the chosen one (the most accurate candidate cheaper than BL if within 2 points of the best, otherwise the best) on the test set, with no search.
