items.raw_text: Strategist : Evolving Reasoning with Agents Taiming Lu 1 Qi Xu 2 Zhigang Hua 2 Zhuang Liu 1 1 Princeton University 2 Meta Abstract A model is only half of an AI agent system. The other half is the inference strategy: the reasoning procedure that turns model calls into a response. Today that second half is written by hand, and the experience of building one strategy never carries to the next. We introduce Strategist , a meta-agent that evolves inference strategies across tasks. Each strategy is written as a blueprint, executable code that other strategies can reuse, and together the blueprints form a library. Given a task and a small development set, Strategist retrieves related blueprints, writes candidate strategies, tests them on real samples, and revises them from the results. Every candidate then enters the library, so later tasks build on earlier discoveries. On 30 benchmarks, Strategist beats the strongest baseline on 24 and matches its average accuracy ( 74.7 % 74.7\% vs. 74.0 % 74.0\% ) at 39% lower inference cost. Its strategies also transfer to unseen tasks and other models without further search. The part of an AI system that is not improved on its own now does. Code Figure 1 : Strategist turns strategy design into a search that accumulates knowledge. Top: in each round, an LLM writes new inference strategies as code, runs them, and stores every one, with its measured accuracy and cost, in a library shared across tasks, so later tasks build on what earlier ones found. The models stay frozen; only the strategies change. Bottom: the search matches the strongest baseline (BL) at lower cost, and its strategies work on new tasks and new models without further search. Cost ratios are per-benchmark averages; transfer costs are totals in USD. Section 1 Introduction Figure 2 : Strategy design is per task; Strategist makes it cumulative. By hand and in prior automated search, nothing carries between tasks. Strategist keeps every strategy in a library that the next task starts from. A model is only half of an AI system. The other half is how that model is put to work, and it matters just as much. Everything from the prompt to the reasoning procedure decides how it behaves. Today that second half is designed by people, fixed, one system at a time. Someone writes the prompt, tries it, adjusts it, and once the system works, the design is left as it is. It is the part of the system that never improves on its own. There is no reason it has to stay that way. The prompts and reasoning procedures that put a model to work are text and code, and agents themselves have become good at writing both. What humans do to design (write, try, adjust) such inference strategies is the natural agentic loop. Such loops have already been shown to evolve programs far beyond their starting point ( Novikov et al., 2025 ) , and AI scientists now run the same loop end to end ( Lu et al., 2024 ; Gottweis et al., 2025 ; Yamada et al., 2025 ) . Designing an inference strategy is the same work with a different object. So why not evolve agentic reasoning itself the same way? Run on far more cases than a person could try, the loop could outdo what people build by hand. Recent work has begun to automate this loop: searching over strategy designs, as raw code or as assemblies of fixed components ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ; Shang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) ; training controllers that route each input to an existing strategy ( Taparia et al., 2026 ; Yue et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Su et al., 2025 ) ; or optimizing one strategy per task by training, evolution, or iterative refinement ( Gao et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) . All of them beat hand-designed strategies on individual benchmarks, and all of them stop there. Searching or routing over a fixed set of strategies can never discover a new one. Trained optimizers need to start over for every task. These methods make the design automatic. We want to make it cumulative (Figure 2 ). We start from the representation. Evolving strategies needs a form open enough to express any reasoning procedure and structured enough for later searches to reuse and combine. We introduce the Strategy Blueprint : an executable program with one shared code interface, so any blueprint can serve as a component inside another. New designs are built from old ones, and the library grows as it is used. On this representation we build Strategist , a meta-agent that does not answer questions but designs the strategies that do. It runs the write, try, adjust loop at scale, with frozen models and no training. Given a task and a small development set, it writes candidate strategies as blueprints, runs them on real samples, reads the traces, and revises them against measured accuracy and cost. Before each round it queries a shared library for relevant blueprints and for diverse ones as inspiration. After each round every candidate goes back into the library with its measurements and experience notes. On 30 benchmarks spanning math, code, commonsense, multi-hop QA, knowledge, logic, and recommendation, we compare Strategist against 18 baselines. Strategist wins on 24 of 30, matching the strongest baseline’s average accuracy ( 74.0 % → 74.7 % 74.0\%\!\to\!74.7\% ) at 39% lower cost. The library pays off on its own: on 10 held-out benchmarks, retrieval with no search stays within 2 points of the strongest baseline on all 10 and beats it on 8 ( 77.8 % → 81.4 % 77.8\%\to 81.4\% ). The same strategies, moved to GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5 without changing a line, still beat the baselines there. Each task solved leaves the next one a better place to start. Until now, only the model in an AI system could learn. Now the rest of it can too. Figure 3 : The Strategy Blueprint is a freeform graph that grows through the library. (a) Two foundations ( chat and agent ) sit at the top. Strategies compose from them and from each other, forming a directed graph whose levels emerge naturally from composition depth. (b) Four protocols govern the graph: every node shares one abstract interface, each node can only call nodes created before it, no cycles are allowed, and no duplicates should exist. Section 2 The Strategy Blueprint Every inference strategy, ultimately, is a program. How it is represented determines what an automated designer can build, test, and reuse. Existing work represents strategies as computation graphs ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Zhuge et al., 2024 ) and declarative pipelines ( Khattab et al., 2024 ; Yue et al., 2026 ) , which are composable but can only express pre-defined patterns, or as monolithic code ( Hu et al., 2025 ) , which can express anything but produces isolated strategies. We introduce the Strategy Blueprint : a reasoning flow that specifies how to solve a task (which models to call, in what order, at which tier, and how) using the open interface of code. Every blueprint exposes the same interface, so any can call any other, and a library can grow by composition. Figure 4 : Strategy blueprint captures reasoning structure. This simplified blueprint example defines the steps, control flow, and the model tier for each step. Prompts are not specified; filling in produces a runnable strategy. Foundations. A blueprint is a Python program that captures the structure of a reasoning strategy without the task-specific prompts. For example, one blueprint defines a loop: generate three candidate answers, review each, then majority-vote. Filling in prompts produces a runnable strategy . It has one interface, execute(llm, task) -> str , and is built from two foundations: chat (single- or multi-turn conversation) and agent (with scaffold and tools). See Figure 4 for an example. Multi-tier model routing. We allow strategies to route across three model tiers ( fast , balanced , complex ), each in two modes ( nothink and thinking ), mirroring the tiered pricing and effort levels of common model providers. Not every reasoning step needs the same intelligence, so each step can target a different tier. This internal routing is what allows a single strategy to be accurate and cost-efficient at the same time. The Blueprint Library. Blueprints live in a shared library that grows over time. They are added along with their measured performance and experience notes on when it works and when it does not. Because every blueprint exposes the same interface, a new blueprint can use any existing one as a component, so the library compounds: early blueprints build on the two foundations, later ones compose from those, and depth grows naturally (Figure 3 a ). Four protocols govern the library (Figure 3 b ): a shared interface, no forward calls, no cycles, and no duplicates. Figure 5 : The Strategist four-stage iterative pipeline. Each iteration: (1) Retrieve relevant blueprints and diverse inspiration from the Library; (2) Propose K K candidates as a mix of new , composed , and reuse blueprints paired with task-specific prompts; (3) Evaluate each candidate, seeing full traces on the training set and aggregated scores on validation; (4) Accumulate the underlying blueprints into the library with measurement cards and experience notes. Section 3 Strategist Given a task and a small development set, Strategist iteratively retrieves relevant blueprints, proposes K = 5 K{=}5 candidates, evaluates them on real samples, and accumulates the results back into the library (Figure 5 ). After N N iterations, the candidate that beats BL on both the validation and hidden splits by the largest hidden-set margin is returned, or BL itself if none does (Algorithm 1 ). Step 1: Retrieve. The strategist queries the Blueprint Library with a short text prompt. The search is hybrid (TF–IDF plus embedding similarity). Each blueprint carries traits, a measurement card, and experience notes written by previous strategists; the search indexes over all of these, so the strategist finds blueprints by measured behavior and prior analyses, not just structural similarity. Beyond relevant results, the library returns adjacent inspiration (blueprints from other domains or reasoning patterns) to inspire new designs. Step 2: Propose. Using the retrieved blueprints and inspiration, the strategist designs new blueprints or composes from existing ones, each paired with task-specific prompts to form candidate strategies. Each blueprint must be one of three kinds: new (a blueprint with no library backbone), composed (a blueprint that wraps or extends an existing one), or reuse (directly applies an existing library blueprint with new prompts). Every iteration includes at least one candidate of each kind, balancing exploration and exploitation. Step 3: Evaluate. The system operates at two levels. At the agent level (inner loop), each candidate strategy processes inputs directly, and the strategist observes the full reasoning trace, execution status, and scores. At the meta level (outer loop), the strategist uses these observations to improve its proposals. The data is split into four parts. The training set : strategies run on these samples and the strategist sees both the scores and the full agent traces. The validation set : strategies also run on these samples, but the strategist sees only the aggregated scores; this mirrors standard train/validation practice and prevents overfitting to the training signal. The hidden set : used to select the winning strategy across all iterations, preventing overfitting to any single iteration. The test set : held out entirely from the search loop and used only for final confirmation. Step 4: Accumulate. The library stores blueprints, not strategies: it retains the reusable structure while discarding task-specific prompts. This is what enables cross-task transfer. After each iteration, the strategist writes an analysis of each candidate’s structural properties and adds the underlying blueprints to the library with their measurement cards and experience notes, with deduplication. From these, 30 randomly selected benchmarks form the main results and 10 are held out for one-shot retrieval. Each benchmark is split into training, validation, and hidden sets of up to 100 samples each, plus a fixed 200-sample test set. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.03601 (cs) [Submitted on 2 Nov 2026] Title: DiabAgent: Toward Agentic Physiological Control Authors: Chengxi Li , Shaoxuan Li , Deyao Hong , Qingle Liu , Yi Huang , Puheng Bian , Minzhi Xu , Lanyue Zhang , Mingze Sun , Xin Li , Calvin Xiao , Shengyuan Wang , Huan-ang Gao , Jiazheng Xu , Kaisen Yang , Hongning Wang View a PDF of the paper titled DiabAgent: Toward Agentic Physiological Control, by Chengxi Li and 15 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: As pretraining scales, medical language models have advanced rapidly in clinical question answering. Their ability to achieve effective physiological control through sustained intervention still lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting: impaired insulin secretion creates dependence on exogenous insulin, with dosing continually adjusted using information about meals, exercise, illness, and glucose measurements. We introduce DiabAgent, a research suite for agentic physiological control comprising the Agentic Physiological Control (APC) framework, the DiabetSim simulator, and the SweetBench benchmark. APC controls glucose through medical-device tools, using ongoing observations to infer individual states, accumulate personal experience, and choose treatment actions. We build DiabetSim to simulate different patients, events, and device conditions for scalable virtual testing and training. Using DiabetSim, we construct SweetBench by instantiating 32 scenario designs as 212 glucose-control tasks. With Claude Opus 5.5 and a fixed decision interval of one hour, APC achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for the open-source closed-loop baseline OpenAPS. Ablations further show that individual adaptation and contextual information improve glucose control. Combining high-frequency rule-based control with lower-frequency agent decisions shows potential for balancing control performance and computational cost. Our work provides a framework, simulator, and evaluation foundation for agents to participate in human physiological control. Their ability to achieve effective physiological control through sustained intervention still lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting: impaired insulin secretion creates dependence on exogenous insulin, with dosing continually adjusted using information about meals, exercise, illness, and glucose measurements. We introduce DiabAgent , a research suite for agentic physiological control comprising the Agentic Physiological Control ( APC ) framework, the DiabetSim simulator, and the SweetBench benchmark. APC controls glucose through medical-device tools, using ongoing observations to infer individual states, accumulate personal experience, and choose treatment actions. We build DiabetSim to simulate different patients, events, and device conditions for scalable virtual testing and training. Using DiabetSim , we construct SweetBench by instantiating 32 scenario designs as 212 glucose-control tasks. With Claude Opus 5.5 and a fixed decision interval of one hour, APC achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for the open-source closed-loop baseline OpenAPS. Ablations further show that individual adaptation and contextual information improve glucose control. Combining high-frequency rule-based control with lower-frequency agent decisions shows potential for balancing control performance and computational cost. Our work provides a framework, simulator, and evaluation foundation for agents to participate in human physiological control. 1 Introduction As pretraining scales, medical language models have advanced rapidly in clinical question answering and treatment advice ( Singhal et al., 2023 ; Arora et al., 2025 ) . Agents combine language models with tools, memory, and environment feedback to execute multi-step tasks ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ) . They complete long tasks in software and service environments and reuse experience in later decisions ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Yao et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Medical agents conduct diagnostic dialogue, analyze treatment options, and operate electronic health records ( Tu et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) . Evaluation of these tasks primarily concerns responses or information operations. Assessing whether language models can control physiology through sustained intervention requires systematic evaluation of the resulting physiological trajectories. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting for this problem. People with type 1 diabetes have impaired insulin secretion and depend on exogenous insulin for glucose control. Dosing needs vary with meals, exercise, illness, and individual states, while insulin continues to act for hours, linking current decisions to earlier treatment and subsequent events ( Holt et al., 2021 ; Riddell et al., 2017 ) . Differences between people, daily changes in insulin needs, and delayed, noisy, or missing glucose measurements make control a long-horizon task requiring ongoing state inference, treatment adjustment, and feedback tracking. Automated insulin delivery and learned closed-loop controllers have advanced glucose control ( Brown et al., 2019 ; Sherr et al., 2022 ; Hettiarachchi et al., 2024 ; Sarkar, 2026 ) . Existing dynamical models and evaluation metrics also provide a basis for simulating glucose dynamics and assessing control outcomes ( Deichmann et al., 2023 ; Battelino et al., 2019 ) . Together, these conditions support systematic study of how agents combine contextual information, personal experience, and device tools for sustained physiological control. Rule-based closed-loop control typically organizes dosing around structured glucose measurements, insulin records, carbohydrate estimates, and prescribed therapy parameters ( OpenAPS community, 2026 ) . Using descriptions of a changed meal plan, illness recovery, or a device problem requires mapping them to predefined inputs and response rules. This mapping constrains how the controller can use cues in free-text context and personal treatment notes. Interacting rare events and individual differences also require judging which cues explain current glucose changes and subsequent dosing needs ( Holt et al., 2021 ) . Can an agent interpret this context and personal experience, act through medical-device tools, and translate that understanding into better physiological control? This question motivates the Agentic Physiological Control ( APC ) framework that we study in DiabAgent . We evaluate APC with five models. With Claude Opus 5.5, it achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for OpenAPS. Further experiments show that records and review support cross-day improvement without weight updates, and that added context can improve control more than increasing agent decision frequency in the tested cases. More frequent agent calls also increase computation. CL-on/off case studies indicate the potential of combining frequent background glucose regulation with less frequent agent decisions that integrate observations and personal experience. Figure 1: APC and its first instantiation. (a) The APC loop, in which an agent acts on a physiological system through device tools and is scored on the physiological outcome. This work applies it to type 1 diabetes, and other systems remain open. (b) DiabetSim combines a physiological engine, device models, and an instance generator; APC acts through the devices and observes their readings. The plot shows a simulated glucose trajectory. (c) SweetBench composes 212 tasks in seven scenario groups and scores the true glucose trajectories, which are hidden from the agent. The donut chart gives the tasks per group, and the bars show the mean COGI of APC with five backend models and of the three baselines. We make three contributions: 1. We introduce APC , an agentic control framework that treats human physiology as an interactive environment, and apply it to glucose control. It acquires information through monitoring devices, delivers medication through medical devices, and adjusts decisions from feedback to optimize glucose-control metrics. 2. We build DiabetSim , a configurable glucose-control simulator that integrates individual physiology, medical devices, events, and observation conditions. It reconstructs the interaction environment faced by APC and provides a foundation for reproducible virtual testing. 3. We construct SweetBench , a benchmark of 212 glucose-control tasks. APC with Claude Opus 5.5 achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for OpenAPS. Further ablations show improved control over days with personal records and end-of-day review. 2 Agentic Physiological Control 2.1 The APC Framework APC treats treatment as a control problem in which the controller is an agent and the sensors and actuators are medical devices. Definition 1 (Agentic Physiological Control) . An APC problem consists of a physiological system with hidden state, medical devices that measure and act on it, reports from the person, and a score on the physiological trajectory. An APC agent repeatedly observes, acts through the devices, and decides when to reassess, so as to maximize the expected score. The state x t x_{t} comprises physiology, device status, and context, and evolves under individual parameters θ \theta . Let d d denote the device configuration and ρ \rho the reporting configuration, which specifies what the person reports, when, and how accurately. Then x t + 1 ∼ P θ ( ⋅ ∣ x t , a t ) , o t ∼ O d , ρ ( ⋅ ∣ x t ) , a t ∈ 𝒜 d ( h t ) . x_{t+1}\sim P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t},a_{t}),\qquad o_{t}\sim O_{d,\rho}(\cdot\mid x_{t}),\qquad a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}_{d}(h_{t}). This is a partially observable Markov decision process ( Kaelbling et al., 1998 ) in which the devices determine both the observation model and the action set. The agent keeps the visible history h t = ( o ≤ t , a < t ) h_{t}=(o_{\leq t},a_{<t}) and a personal record M t M_{t} summarizing past interaction with the same individual, and selects actions with a policy π ⁡ ( a t ∣ h t , M t ) \pi(a_{t}\mid h_{t},M_{t}) . The score is computed from the true physiological variables m t = f ⁡ ( x t ) m_{t}=f(x_{t}) , which the agent never observes directly. Over a horizon T T , the objective is max π 𝔼 π [ S ( m 0 : T ) ] \max_{\pi}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[S(m_{0:T})] . An APC agent has four components that close this loop (Figure 2 ). Decision making selects an intervention, a measurement, or waiting, and states its rationale. Device tools execute the operation and return readings and delivery logs. Monitoring watches incoming observations and returns control to the agent when its chosen waiting interval ends or a specified condition occurs. The personal record carries what has been learned about the individual into later decisions. The design addresses three requirements. Interpretability makes the basis of an action traceable through decision rules or an explicit rationale. Information integration combines glucose measurements, natural-language and multimodal reports, and personal history to infer the hidden state and select interventions. Long-tail event adaptation uses contextual reports to adjust treatment when events overlap or fall outside predefined response categories. To instantiate APC in a new domain, one specifies the physiological variables and the score S S , the devices with their observation models and operations ( O d , ρ O_{d,\rho} , 𝒜 d \mathcal{A}_{d} ), the reports the person can provide, and an environment in which agents can be evaluated safely. Section 2.2 makes these choices for type 1 diabetes, and Sections 3 and 4 build the environment and the tasks. Figure 2: The APC loop. The agent reaches the physiological system only through medical devices. Sensor readings and the person’s reports return through monitoring, which wakes the agent at its chosen time or when a trigger fires, and the personal record persists across decisions and days. The score S S is computed from the true physiological trajectory. 2.2 Glucose Control Rule-based glucose controllers organize dosing around structured glucose and therapy records ( Holt et al., 2021 ; OpenAPS community, 2026 ) . LLM-T1D distills a reinforcement-learning policy into a language model that doses insulin and explains its decisions ( Sarkar, 2026 ) . We instantiate APC for glucose control in type 1 diabetes, combining device observations with contextual reports and personal experience. The state comprises glucose, insulin still acting, carbohydrate absorption, and device status; meals, activity, and illness perturb this state. APC observes sensor or meter readings, delivery logs and alarms, and reports of meals, activity, and device problems. Its actions are insulin delivery through boluses, temporary basal rates, or injections, measurement requests such as scans and fingersticks, device management such as cancellation, suspension, and resumption, and waiting. The score combines time in range, hypoglycemia, and variability of true glucose (Section 4.2 ; Battelino et al., 2019 ). The idealized reference is a healthy pancreas, which regulates glucose continuously without devices or reports. At each decision, APC reviews recent readings, insulin still acting, reported events, and its personal record, and estimates where glucose is heading. It then chooses one operation supported by the current devices and states why. The same decision fixes when to look again and which events, such as a new reading, a reported meal, or an alarm, should wake it earlier. Monitoring holds control until one of these occurs. The personal record stores notes on how this individual has responded to meals, activity, and insulin. In multi-day episodes the conversation resets each day while the record persists, and revised therapy settings persist where the experimental condition allows. Adaptation therefore happens through experience with model weights fixed, and Section 5.3.1 evaluates the effect of keeping the record. Appendix B specifies the observation and action interface. 3 DiabetSim DiabetSim is a configurable environment for virtual testing of glucose-control agents. It comprises a physiological engine, monitoring and delivery device models, and an instance generator. Together, these components simulate individual glucose responses, everyday events, and device-mediated interventions. Agents observe device readings and event reports; the evaluator records the underlying glucose trajectory for scoring. 3.1 Simulator Engine The engine models glucose–insulin dynamics using Deichmann et al. (2023) , including the effects of physical activity. Individual parameters θ \theta specify insulin sensitivity and body-mass-dependent responses. The simulator includes eight physiological types with different body masses and dawn phenomena, together with day-to-day variation in insulin sensitivity. Meals introduce carbohydrate absorption, while activity and illness modify subsequent physiological responses. The simulator configures therapy settings separately from physiological parameters, allowing prescribed treatment to differ from an individual’s insulin requirements. An event-driven scheduler advances physiological and device states as external events occur and treatment actions execute. 3.2 Devices Observation. Monitoring devices determine the measurements available to the agent. The simulator includes eight sensor models and six glucose-meter models, parameterized by published accuracy specifications ( Vettoretti et al., 2019 ; International Organization for Standardization, 2013 ) . Real-time continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) produce readings every five minutes; flash sensors return readings upon scanning, and meters upon fingerstick measurement. The models represent sensor warm-up, data gaps, and compression artifacts. Scans and fingerstick measurements are agent actions, making observation timing part of the control policy. A reporting configuration ρ \rho additionally specifies the availability, timing, and accuracy of reports about meals, activity, and other events. Action set. Delivery devices determine the available treatment operations and their constraints. The simulator includes five pump models, 10 pen models, and 10 insulin formulations. Each device configuration d d defines an action set 𝒜 d \mathcal{A}_{d} : pumps support device-specific subsets of boluses, temporary basal rates, extended boluses, cancellation, and suspension or resumption; pens support discrete injections. Insulin formulations determine the corresponding absorption and action profiles. The device interface validates commands against dose increments, dose limits, bolus intervals, and device state, and records rejected commands with their reasons. Occlusions and suspension alter actual delivery, separating the requested intervention from the dose received. 3.3 Instance Generation An instance specifies patient parameters, device and reporting configurations, the event schedule, initial physiological and device states, pre-episode history, evaluation horizon, and random seed. The generator assigns representative parameter values or samples from configured ranges, then combines these specifications to produce instances with different patients, devices, events, and observation conditions. Event combinations, timing, and magnitude are configurable independently of the patient and device parameters. Saving the resolved specification fixes the initialization, external event schedule, and random seed for replay and comparisons between controllers. 4 SweetBench SweetBench turns DiabetSim into a fixed set of 212 evaluation tasks. Each task is a fixed patient–scenario configuration that specifies an individual, an event calendar, the devices, the information available to the agent, the initial state, and the horizon, and each is scored on the true glucose trajectory. Existing medical benchmarks score answers, records, or plans for a single encounter or a supplied history. SweetBench instead scores multi-day control in which the agent’s actions shape what it observes next, and it computes every score programmatically from the true trajectory (Table 1 ). Table 1: Task scope and scoring in medical benchmarks. Benchmark Long-horizon control Verifiable score Evaluation tasks HealthBench ( Arora et al., 2025 ) – ∘ \circ Medical QA AgentClinic ( Schmidgall et al., 2024 ) – ∘ \circ Diagnostic dialogue MedAgentBench ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) – ✓ \checkmark EHR tasks LongMedBench ( Xu et al., 2026 ) ∘ \circ ✓ \checkmark Longitudinal clinical reasoning DM-Bench ( Cardei et al., 2025 ) ∘ \circ ∘ \circ Diabetes QA and planning HealthLoopQA ( Niu et al., 2026 ) ∘ \circ ✓ \checkmark Time-series QA SweetBench (ours) ✓ \checkmark ✓ \checkmark Closed-loop glucose control Long-horizon control: ✓ \checkmark , multi-day interventions with action-dependent physiological feedback; ∘ \circ , reasoning or planning over longitudinal records; –, encounter-level tasks. Verifiable score: ✓ \checkmark , fully programmatic scoring against references or rules; ∘ \circ , includes model-based semantic grading. 4.1 Task Design Within DiabetSim ’s configurable environment space, SweetBench defines 32 scenario designs in seven groups. These cover meal timing and absorption, residual insulin, exercise, changing insulin needs, pump under-delivery, sensor errors, and illness recovery (Table 2 ). Each design specifies an event combination and its temporal relationships. Examples include a cancelled meal after a pre-meal bolus followed by activity, or silent under-delivery with upward sensor drift. We instantiate each design for four to eight simulated individuals, adapting event timing and magnitude to each person, to obtain 212 tasks. Appendix A , Table 8 , lists all designs by ID, including A01 and E03. Table 2: Scenario groups of SweetBench . Each design yields tasks for four to eight individuals. Appendix A lists all 32 designs. Group Example design Designs Tasks A Meal timing and absorption A03: a meal cancelled after pre-bolusing, followed by activity 4 28 B Insulin from earlier doses B01: repeated doses after a small meal overlap as absorption ends 4 28 C Exercise C04: breakfast and lunch skipped during prolonged aerobic activity 4 24 D Changing insulin needs D02: needs returning after sleep loss and the dawn phenomenon 6 38 E Pump under-delivery E04: silent under-delivery with progressively false-high sensor readings 4 28 F Sensor errors F06: missed meals and exercise causing lows masked by positive sensor bias 6 36 H Illness and recovery H03: insulin needs recover before appetite returns 4 30 Total 32 212 In the default setting, a task is a 72-hour episode with a Dana-i pump delivering insulin aspart and real-time CGM with sensor error and delay, under information condition I2 described below. Because a configuration fixes the individual, the event calendar, and the random seed, the same task can also be run with other delivery devices, information conditions, or decision schedules, and a seven-day version of selected designs supports multi-day evaluation with the same individual and personal record (Section 5.3.1 ). Section 5.3 uses these variants. Information conditions. The reporting configuration ρ \rho takes three levels. Under I2, the agent receives sensor glucose, the device state needed to operate the pump, records of its own actions, and estimates derived from these records, and meals and other events are not reported. I1 adds the time and carbohydrate content of each meal. I0 further adds free-text reports, such as stated meal plans and descriptions of upcoming events. 4.2 Metrics All metrics use the true glucose trajectory sampled every 5 minutes. Let g 1 , … , g n g_{1},\ldots,g_{n} denote these samples in mg/dL. We compute time in range TIR = 100 n − 1 ∑ j = 1 n 𝟏 { 72.064 ≤ g j ≤ 144.128 } \mathrm{TIR}=100n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{72.064\leq g_{j}\leq 144.128\} and time below range TBR = 100 n − 1 ∑ j = 1 n 𝟏 { g j < 70 } \mathrm{TBR}=100n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{g_{j}<70\} as percentages. TIR uses 4–8 mmol/L (72.064–144.128 mg/dL) throughout the main experiments and ablations. This range is tighter than the consensus target and is specific to the benchmark, while the hypoglycemia threshold of 70 mg/dL follows the CGM consensus ( Battelino et al., 2019 ) . The glucose standard deviation is σ g = n − 1 ​ ∑ j = 1 n ( g j − g ¯ ) 2 \sigma_{g}=\sqrt{n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(g_{j}-\bar{g})^{2}} , where g ¯ = n − 1 ​ ∑ j = 1 n g j \bar{g}=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}g_{j} . Overall score. We adapt COGI, which combines time in range, hypoglycemia, and glucose variability with weights of 0.50, 0.35, and 0.15 ( Leelarathna et al., 2020 ) . Our research variant COGI-4-8 (abbreviated COGI below) replaces the published 70–180 mg/dL TIR band with 4–8 mmol/L, while retaining the hypoglycemia and population-SD components. Let c ⁡ ( x ) = min ⁡ ( 1 , max ⁡ ( 0 , x ) ) c(x)=\min(1,\max(0,x)) . Its three subscores are S TIR \displaystyle S_{\mathrm{TIR}} = TIR , \displaystyle=\mathrm{TIR}, S Hypo \displaystyle S_{\mathrm{Hypo}} = 100 ​ c ​ ( 1 − TBR 15 ) , \displaystyle=100\,c\!\left(1-\frac{\mathrm{TBR}}{15}\right), S GV \displaystyle S_{\mathrm{GV}} = 100 ​ c ​ ( 108 − σ g 90 ) . \displaystyle=100\,c\!\left(\frac{108-\sigma_{g}}{90}\right). The hypoglycemia subscore decreases from 100 at zero TBR to zero at 15% TBR. The variability subscore decreases from 100 at a standard deviation of 18 mg/dL to zero at 108 mg/dL. The overall score is S = 0.50 ​ S TIR + 0.35 ​ S Hypo + 0.15 ​ S GV . S=0.50S_{\mathrm{TIR}}+0.35S_{\mathrm{Hypo}}+0.15S_{\mathrm{GV}}. COGI and all three subscores range from 0 to 100, with higher values indicating better control. Results report their means across episodes with equal weight per task. 5 Experiments 5.1 Setting Protocol. We evaluate all methods on the 212 tasks of SweetBench . Each 72-hour episode fixes the patient, initial state, event calendar, and random seed, and uses a simulated Dana-i pump, insulin aspart, and real-time CGM under I2. Meals and other events remain unreported. Each method acts through the same device interface using only visible measurements and records; the environment continues to evolve between decisions. The main evaluation adds no separate background HCL controller. We compute COGI and its three subscores from 864 five-minute true-glucose samples per episode, then average completed episodes with equal weight (Section 4.2 ). Baseline Setting. We compare three controllers. Basal–Bolus (BB) follows a prescribed basal schedule and calculates meal and correction boluses from reported carbohydrates, glucose, carbohydrate ratio, insulin sensitivity, and insulin on board ( Holt et al., 2021 ; Fox et al., 2020 ) . Event-Aware Basal–Bolus (BB+Rules) augments this BB policy with predefined rules for glucose trends, reported exercise and illness, and device problems ( Riddell et al., 2017 ) . OpenAPS uses its open-source dosing core to compute temporary basal adjustments and micro-boluses from glucose feedback. All three controllers use 15-minute decision intervals and the same visible observations. They complete long tasks in software and service environments and reuse experience in later decisions ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Yao et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Medical agents conduct diagnostic dialogue, analyze treatment options, and operate electronic health records ( Tu et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) . Evaluation of these tasks primarily concerns responses or information operations. Assessing whether language models can control physiology through sustained intervention requires systematic evaluation of the resulting physiological trajectories. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting for this problem. People with type 1 diabetes have impaired insulin secretion and depend on exogenous insulin for glucose control. Dosing needs vary with meals, exercise, illness, and individual states, while insulin continues to act for hours, linking current decisions to earlier treatment and subsequent events ( Holt et al., 2021 ; Riddell et al., 2017 ) . Differences between people, daily changes in insulin needs, and delayed, noisy, or missing glucose measurements make control a long-horizon task requiring ongoing state inference, treatment adjustment, and feedback tracking. Automated insulin delivery and learned closed-loop controllers have advanced glucose control ( Brown et al., 2019 ; Sherr et al., 2022 ; Hettiarachchi et al., 2024 ; Sarkar, 2026 ) . Existing dynamical models and evaluation metrics also provide a basis for simulating glucose dynamics and assessing control outcomes ( Deichmann et al., 2023 ; Battelino et al., 2019 ) . Together, these conditions support systematic study of how agents combine contextual information, personal experience, and device tools for sustained physiological control. Rule-based closed-loop control typically organizes dosing around structured glucose measurements, insulin records, carbohydrate estimates, and prescribed therapy parameters ( OpenAPS community, 2026 ) . Using descriptions of a changed meal plan, illness recovery, or a device problem requires mapping them to predefined inputs and response rules. This mapping constrains how the controller can use cues in free-text context and personal treatment notes. Interacting rare events and individual differences also require judging which cues explain current glucose changes and subsequent dosing needs ( Holt et al., 2021 ) . Can an agent interpret this context and personal experience, act through medical-device tools, and translate that understanding into better physiological control? This question motivates the Agentic Physiological Control ( APC ) framework that we study in DiabAgent . We evaluate APC with five models. With Claude Opus 5.5, it achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for OpenAPS. Further experiments show that records and review support cross-day improvement without weight updates, and that added context can improve control more than increasing agent decision frequency in the tested cases. More frequent agent calls also increase computation. CL-on/off case studies indicate the potential of combining frequent background glucose regulation with less frequent agent decisions that integrate observations and personal experience. Figure 1: APC and its first instantiation. (a) The APC loop, in which an agent acts on a physiological system through device tools and is scored on the physiological outcome. This work applies it to type 1 diabetes, and other systems remain open. (b) DiabetSim combines a physiological engine, device models, and an instance generator; APC acts through the devices and observes their readings. The plot shows a simulated glucose trajectory. (c) SweetBench composes 212 tasks in seven scenario groups and scores the true glucose trajectories, which are hidden from the agent. The donut chart gives the tasks per group, and the bars show the mean COGI of APC with five backend models and of the three baselines. We make three contributions: 1. We introduce APC , an agentic control framework that treats human physiology as an interactive environment, and apply it to glucose control. It acquires information through monitoring devices, delivers medication through medical devices, and adjusts decisions from feedback to optimize glucose-control metrics. 2. We build DiabetSim , a configurable glucose-control simulator that integrates individual physiology, medical devices, events, and observation conditions. It reconstructs the interaction environment faced by APC and provides a foundation for reproducible virtual testing. 3. We construct SweetBench , a benchmark of 212 glucose-control tasks. APC with Claude Opus 5.5 achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for OpenAPS. Further ablations show improved control over days with personal records and end-of-day review. 2 Agentic Physiological Control 2.1 The APC Framework APC treats treatment as a control problem in which the controller is an agent and the sensors and actuators are medical devices. Definition 1 (Agentic Physiological Control) . An APC problem consists of a physiological system with hidden state, medical devices that measure and act on it, reports from the person, and a score on the physiological trajectory. An APC agent repeatedly observes, acts through the devices, and decides when to reassess, so as to maximize the expected score. The state x t x_{t} comprises physiology, device status, and context, and evolves under individual parameters θ \theta . Let d d denote the device configuration and ρ \rho the reporting configuration, which specifies what the person reports, when, and how accurately. Then x t + 1 ∼ P θ ( ⋅ ∣ x t , a t ) , o t ∼ O d , ρ ( ⋅ ∣ x t ) , a t ∈ 𝒜 d ( h t ) . x_{t+1}\sim P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t},a_{t}),\qquad o_{t}\sim O_{d,\rho}(\cdot\mid x_{t}),\qquad a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}_{d}(h_{t}). This is a partially observable Markov decision process ( Kaelbling et al., 1998 ) in which the devices determine both the observation model and the action set. The agent keeps the visible history h t = ( o ≤ t , a < t ) h_{t}=(o_{\leq t},a_{<t}) and a personal record M t M_{t} summarizing past interaction with the same individual, and selects actions with a policy π ⁡ ( a t ∣ h t , M t ) \pi(a_{t}\mid h_{t},M_{t}) . The score is computed from the true physiological variables m t = f ⁡ ( x t ) m_{t}=f(x_{t}) , which the agent never observes directly. Over a horizon T T , the objective is max π 𝔼 π [ S ( m 0 : T ) ] \max_{\pi}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[S(m_{0:T})] . An APC agent has four components that close this loop (Figure 2 ). Decision making selects an intervention, a measurement, or waiting, and states its rationale. Device tools execute the operation and return readings and delivery logs. Monitoring watches incoming observations and returns control to the agent when its chosen waiting interval ends or a specified condition occurs. The personal record carries what has been learned about the individual into later decisions. The design addresses three requirements. Interpretability makes the basis of an action traceable through decision rules or an explicit rationale. Information integration combines glucose measurements, natural-language and multimodal reports, and personal history to infer the hidden state and select interventions. Long-tail event adaptation uses contextual reports to adjust treatment when events overlap or fall outside predefined response categories. To instantiate APC in a new domain, one specifies the physiological variables and the score S S , the devices with their observation models and operations ( O d , ρ O_{d,\rho} , 𝒜 d \mathcal{A}_{d} ), the reports the person can provide, and an environment in which agents can be evaluated safely. Section 2.2 makes these choices for type 1 diabetes, and Sections 3 and 4 build the environment and the tasks. Figure 2: The APC loop. The agent reaches the physiological system only through medical devices. Sensor readings and the person’s reports return through monitoring, which wakes the agent at its chosen time or when a trigger fires, and the personal record persists across decisions and days. The score S S is computed from the true physiological trajectory. 2.2 Glucose Control Rule-based glucose controllers organize dosing around structured glucose and therapy records ( Holt et al., 2021 ; OpenAPS community, 2026 ) . LLM-T1D distills a reinforcement-learning policy into a language model that doses insulin and explains its decisions ( Sarkar, 2026 ) . We instantiate APC for glucose control in type 1 diabetes, combining device observations with contextual reports and personal experience. The state comprises glucose, insulin still acting, carbohydrate absorption, and device status; meals, activity, and illness perturb this state. APC observes sensor or meter readings, delivery logs and alarms, and reports of meals, activity, and device problems. Its actions are insulin delivery through boluses, temporary basal rates, or injections, measurement requests such as scans and fingersticks, device management such as cancellation, suspension, and resumption, and waiting. The score combines time in range, hypoglycemia, and variability of true glucose (Section 4.2 ; Battelino et al., 2019 ). The idealized reference is a healthy pancreas, which regulates glucose continuously without devices or reports. At each decision, APC reviews recent readings, insulin still acting, reported events, and its personal record, and estimates where glucose is heading. It then chooses one operation supported by the current devices and states why. The same decision fixes when to look again and which events, such as a new reading, a reported meal, or an alarm, should wake it earlier. Monitoring holds control until one of these occurs. The personal record stores notes on how this individual has responded to meals, activity, and insulin. In multi-day episodes the conversation resets each day while the record persists, and revised therapy settings persist where the experimental condition allows. Adaptation therefore happens through experience with model weights fixed, and Section 5.3.1 evaluates the effect of keeping the record. Appendix B specifies the observation and action interface. 3 DiabetSim DiabetSim is a configurable environment for virtual testing of glucose-control agents. It comprises a physiological engine, monitoring and delivery device models, and an instance generator. Together, these components simulate individual glucose responses, everyday events, and device-mediated interventions. Agents observe device readings and event reports; the evaluator records the underlying glucose trajectory for scoring. 3.1 Simulator Engine The engine models glucose–insulin dynamics using Deichmann et al. (2023) , including the effects of physical activity. Individual parameters θ \theta specify insulin sensitivity and body-mass-dependent responses. The simulator includes eight physiological types with different body masses and dawn phenomena, together with day-to-day variation in insulin sensitivity. Meals introduce carbohydrate absorption, while activity and illness modify subsequent physiological responses. The simulator configures therapy settings separately from physiological parameters, allowing prescribed treatment to differ from an individual’s insulin requirements. An event-driven scheduler advances physiological and device states as external events occur and treatment actions execute. 3.2 Devices Observation. Monitoring devices determine the measurements available to the agent. The simulator includes eight sensor models and six glucose-meter models, parameterized by published accuracy specifications ( Vettoretti et al., 2019 ; International Organization for Standardization, 2013 ) . Real-time continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) produce readings every five minutes; flash sensors return readings upon scanning, and meters upon fingerstick measurement. The models represent sensor warm-up, data gaps, and compression artifacts. Scans and fingerstick measurements are agent actions, making observation timing part of the control policy. A reporting configuration ρ \rho additionally specifies the availability, timing, and accuracy of reports about meals, activity, and other events. Action set. Delivery devices determine the available treatment operations and their constraints. The simulator includes five pump models, 10 pen models, and 10 insulin formulations. Each device configuration d d defines an action set 𝒜 d \mathcal{A}_{d} : pumps support device-specific subsets of boluses, temporary basal rates, extended boluses, cancellation, and suspension or resumption; pens support discrete injections. Insulin formulations determine the corresponding absorption and action profiles. The device interface validates commands against dose increments, dose limits, bolus intervals, and device state, and records rejected commands with their reasons. Occlusions and suspension alter actual delivery, separating the requested intervention from the dose received. 3.3 Instance Generation An instance specifies patient parameters, device and reporting configurations, the event schedule, initial physiological and device states, pre-episode history, evaluation horizon, and random seed. The generator assigns representative parameter values or samples from configured ranges, then combines these specifications to produce instances with different patients, devices, events, and observation conditions. Event combinations, timing, and magnitude are configurable independently of the patient and device parameters. Saving the resolved specification fixes the initialization, external event schedule, and random seed for replay and comparisons between controllers. 4 SweetBench SweetBench turns DiabetSim into a fixed set of 212 evaluation tasks. Each task is a fixed patient–scenario configuration that specifies an individual, an event calendar, the devices, the information available to the agent, the initial state, and the horizon, and each is scored on the true glucose trajectory. Existing medical benchmarks score answers, records, or plans for a single encounter or a supplied history. SweetBench instead scores multi-day control in which the agent’s actions shape what it observes next, and it computes every score programmatically from the true trajectory (Table 1 ). I1 adds the time and carbohydrate content of each meal. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.03600 (cs) [Submitted on 2 Nov 2026] Title: Four Bridges: Measuring Deception Propensity in a Multi-Agent Game Authors: Raphael Casey , Michael Simeone , Alberto Tosato , Florian Ernst , Kemal El Moujahid , James Tamplin , Tommaso Tosato View a PDF of the paper titled Four Bridges: Measuring Deception Propensity in a Multi-Agent Game, by Raphael Casey and 6 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they interact and coordinate with other agents, yet honesty is mostly measured in single-turn, single-agent benchmarks that pressure the model to deceive. We study deception that emerges in multi-agent interaction without any instruction to deceive. We introduce Kradle, a platform for evaluating AI models, and Four Bridges, an information asymmetry game in which four agents distribute across four rooms: one is the death room, the others hold food worth more if not shared. One agent, the informed agent, knows which room is the death room and can withhold or disclose that information. We evaluate eight frontier models as the informed agent. Deceptive behavior appears in every model and in 73% of all runs (6% to 100% per model), and does not decrease with capability tier within a model family. When the informed agent does disclose, the warning is often challenged, and agents that challenge it enter the death room twice as often as those that do not. Telling all agents that one of them knows the death room collapses deception in six of eight models; telling the informed agent that the room is permanently fatal moves only one. On an open-weight model, an honesty steering vector reduces deception to 0% and adversarial honesty training to 6%. The platform and game provide a testbed for measuring deceptive behavior and comparing interventions. From February 18, 2002, to February 9, 2006, the U.S. Treasury published a factor for adjusting the daily nominal 20-year constant maturity in order to estimate a 30-year nominal rate. Based on the unweighted average bid yields for all TIPS with remaining terms to maturity of more than 10 years. Note: Current and historical H.15 data, along with weekly, monthly, and annual averages, are available on the Board's Data Download Program (DDP) at www.federalreserve.gov/datadownload/Choose.aspx?rel=H15 ). Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 03, 2026 Back to Top

From February 18, 2002, to February 9, 2006, the U.S. Treasury published a factor for adjusting the daily nominal 20-year constant maturity in order to estimate a 30-year nominal rate. The historical adjustment factor can be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . Source: U.S. Treasury. 10. Yields on Treasury inflation protected securities (TIPS) adjusted to constant maturities. Source: U.S. Treasury. Additional information on both nominal and inflation-indexed yields may be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . 11. Based on the unweighted average bid yields for all TIPS with remaining terms to maturity of more than 10 years. Note: Current and historical H.15 data, along with weekly, monthly, and annual averages, are available on the Board's Data Download Program (DDP) at www.federalreserve.gov/datadownload/Choose.aspx?rel=H15 ). Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 03, 2026 Back to Top
